Mr. President of the General Assembly, Mr. President of the Human Rights Council, High Commissioner, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, We begin this session under the weight of a grim milestone, the third anniversary of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in violation of the UN Charter. More than 12,600 civilians killed, with many more injured. Entire communities reduced to rubble, hospitals and schools destroyed. We must spare no effort to bring an end to this conflict and to achieve a just and lasting peace in line with UN Charter, international law, and General Assembly resolutions. Conflicts like the war in Ukraine exact a heavy toll. a toll on people, a toll on fundamental principles like territorial integrity, sovereignty, and the rule of law, and a toll on the vital business of this Council. Without respect for human rights, civil, cultural, economic, political, and social, sustainable peace is a pipe dream. And like this Council, human rights shine a light in the darkest places. Through your work, and the work of the High Commissioner's Office around the world, you are supporting brave human rights defenders risking persecution, detention, and even death. You are working with governments, civil society, and others to strengthen action on human rights, and you are supporting investigations and accountability. Five years ago, we launched our call to action for human rights embedding human rights across the work of the United Nations around the world in close cooperation with our partners. I will continue supporting this important work and the High Commissioner's Office as we fight for human rights everywhere. Excellencies, we have our work cut out for us. Human rights are the oxygen of humanity, but one by one, human rights are being suffocated. By autocrats, crushing opposition because they fear what a truly empowered people would do. By a patriarchy that keeps girls out of school and women at arm's length from basic rights. By wars and violence that strip populations of their right to food, water, and education. by warmongers who thumb their nose at international law, international humanitarian law, and UN Charter. Human rights are being suffocated by the climate crisis and by a morally bankrupt global financial system that too often obstructs the path to greater equality and sustainable development. By runaway technologies like artificial intelligence that hold great promise but also the ability to violate human rights at the touch of a button. By growing intolerance against entire groups, from indigenous peoples to migrants and refugees, to the LGBTQI+ community, to persons with disabilities. And by voices of division and anger who view human rights not as a boon to humanity, but as a barrier to the power, profit, and control they seek. In short, human rights are on the ropes and being pummeled hard. And this represents a direct threat to all of the hard work, mechanisms, and systems established over the last 80 years to protect and advance human rights. But as the recently adopted Pact for the Future reminds us, human rights are in fact a source of solutions. And the pact provides a playbook on how we can win the fight for human rights on several fronts. First, human rights through peace and peace through human rights. Conflicts inflict human rights violations on a massive scale. In the occupied Palestinian territory, Violations of human rights have skyrocketed since the horrific Hamas attacks of October 7 and the intolerable levels of deaths and destruction in Gaza. And I am gravely concerned by the rising violence in the occupied West Bank by Israel settlers and other violations, as well as calls for annexation. We are witnessing a precarious ceasefire. We must avoid at all costs a resumption of hostilities. The people in Gaza have already suffered too much. It's time for a permanent ceasefire, the dignified release of all remaining hostages, irreversible progress towards a two-state solution, an end to the occupation, and the establishment of an independent Palestinian state with Gaza as an integral part. In Sudan, bloodshed, displacement, and famine are engulfing the country. The warring parties must take immediate action to protect civilians, uphold human rights, cease hostilities, and forge peace. And domestic and international human rights monitoring and investigation mechanisms should be permitted to document what's happening on the ground. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, we see a deadly whirlwind of violence and horrifying human rights abuses. amplified by the recent M23 offensive supported by the Rwandan Defense Forces. As more cities fall, the risk of a regional war rises. It's time to silence the guns. It's time for diplomacy and dialogue. The recent joint summit in Tanzania offered a way forward with a renewed call for an immediate ceasefire. The sovereignty and territorial integrity of the DRC must be respected. The Congolese people deserve peace. In the Sahel, I call for a renewed regional dialogue to protect citizens from terrorism and systemic violations of human rights, and to create the conditions for sustainable development. In Myanmar, the situation has grown far worse in the four years since the military seized power and arbitrarily detained members of the democratically elected government. We need greater cooperation to bring an end to the hostilities and forge a path towards an inclusive democratic transition and the return to civilian rule, allowing for the safe return of the Rohingya refugees. And in Haiti, we are seeing massive human rights violations, including more than a million people displaced and children facing a horrific increase in sexual violence and recruitment into gangs. In the coming days, I will put forward proposals to the United Nations Security Council for greater stability and security for the people of Haiti, namely through an effective UN assistance mechanism to support the Multilateral Security Support Mission, the national police, and Haitian authorities. A durable solution requires a political process led and owned by the Haitian people that restores democratic institutions through elections. The Pact for the Future calls for peace processes and approaches rooted in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, international law, and UN Charter. It proposes specific actions to prioritize conflict prevention, mediation, resolution, and peacebuilding, and includes a commitment to tackle the root causes of conflict, which so often in denials of basic human needs and rights. Second, the Pact for the Future advances human rights through development. Sustainable development goals and human rights are fundamentally intertwined. They represent real human needs, health, food, water, education, decent work, and social protection. With less than one fifth of the goals on track, The pact calls for a massive acceleration through an SDG stimulus, reforming the global financial architecture, and taking meaningful actions for countries drowning in debt. This must include focused action to conquer the most widespread human rights abuse in history, inequality for women and girls. The pact calls for investing in battling all forms of discrimination and violence against women and girls and ensuring their meaningful participation and leadership across all walks of life. And along with the declaration on future generations, the pact calls for supporting the rights and futures of young people through decent work, removing barriers for youth participation, and enhancing training. And the Global Digital Compact calls on nations to champion young innovators, nurture entrepreneurial spirit, and to equip the next generation with digital literacy and skills. Third, the Pact for the Future recognizes that the rule of law and human rights go hand in hand. The rule of law, when founded on human rights, is an essential pillar of protection. It shields the most vulnerable. It's the first line of defense against crime and corruption. It supports fair, just, and inclusive economies and societies. It holds perpetrators of human rights atrocities to account. It enables civic space for people to make their voices heard and for journalists to carry on their essential work free from interference or threats. and reaffirms the world's commitment to equal access to justice, good governance, and transparent and accountable institutions.

Fourthly, we must achieve human rights through climate action. Last year was the hottest on record and comes on the back of the hottest decade on record. Rising heat, melting glaciers, and warmer oceans are a recipe for disaster. Floods, droughts, deadly storms, mass displacement. Hunger, our war on nature, is also a war on human rights. We must choose a different path. I pay tribute to the many Member States who legally recognise the right to a healthy environment, and I call on all countries to follow suit. Governments must keep their promise to produce new economy-wide national climate action plans this year, and this has to be done well ahead of COP30 to be held in Brazil. These plans must limit the rising global temperature to 1.5 degrees, including by speeding up the global energy transition. We also need a massive surge in financing for climate action in developing countries so that we can adapt to global warming slash emissions and speed up the renewables revolution, which offers massive economic opportunities. And we must stand up to the misleading campaign undertaken by many in the fossil fuel industries and its enablers who are aiding and abetting this madness. And at the same time, we must protect and defend those on the front lines of climate justice. And fifth, human rights through stronger, better governance of technology. Fast moving technologies are now encroaching on every aspect of our lives. This deeply troubles me about human rights being undermined as well. At its best, social media is a meeting place for people to exchange ideas and to trigger respectful debate. But it can also be the stage for fiery combat and blatant ignorance. It's a place where the poisons of misinformation, disinformation, racism, misogyny and hate speech are not just tolerated, but often encouraged. Online verbal violence can easily turn into physical violence in the real world. Recent rollbacks on fact-checking and content moderation online are opening the floodgates once more to more hate, threats and violence. Make no mistake, these rollbacks will actually lead to less free speech and not more. because people are becoming more and more afraid of expressing their opinions on these platforms. Meanwhile, the huge promise of artificial intelligence goes hand in hand with the unfathomable peril to undermine human autonomy, identity and control, and yes, human rights as well. In the face of these threats, the Global Digital Compact brings the world together to ensure that human rights will not be sacrificed on the altar of technology. This includes working with digital companies and policymakers to extend human rights to every corner of cyberspace, including through a new focus on information integrity across all digital platforms. The Global Principles for Information Integrity that I launched last year will support and underpin these efforts as we push for a more humane information ecosystem. The Global Digital Compact also includes the first universal agreement on the governance of artificial intelligence that brings every country to the table and sets commitments on capacity building so that all countries and people can benefit from the potential of artificial intelligence. We need to invest, though, in affordable internet, digital literacy and infrastructure. By helping developing countries to use artificial intelligence to grow small businesses, improve public services and connect communities to new markets, and by placing human rights at the center of AI-driven systems. The pact's decisions to create an independent international scientific panel on AI and ongoing global dialogue that ensures that all countries have a voice in shaping its future are important steps forward. We must implement them. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, We can help end the suffocation of human rights by breathing life into the Pact for the Future and the work of this Council. Let's do it together. We have no time to lose. I thank you.

President, Secretary General, distinguished delegates, the international system is going through a tectonic shift. and the human rights edifice we have built up so painstakingly over decades has never been under so much strain. Today, we mark the third anniversary of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine at a time of escalating civilian casualties, continued wanton destruction of urban areas, and speculation about the war's trajectory. Any sustainable peace must be anchored in the rights, needs, and aspirations of the Ukrainian people, in accountability, and in the principles of the United Nations Charter and international law. The decisions that are made today, whether they foster justice or impunity, will shape what follows. In Israel and the occupied Palestinian territory, where the suffering has been unbearable, I repeat my call for an independent investigation into grave violations of international law committed by Israel in the course of its attacks across Gaza and by Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. Any sustainable solution must be based on accountability, on justice, the right to self-determination, and the human rights and dignity of both Israelis and Palestinians. Any suggestion of forcing people from their land is completely unacceptable. Mr. President, Excellencies, beyond Ukraine and Gaza, conflicts and crises are tearing communities and societies apart, from Sudan to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, Myanmar, and Afghanistan. Social tensions are rising, as inequalities and injustices breed resentment, often directed at refugees, at migrants, and the most vulnerable. Perversely, the richest 1% control more wealth than the majority of humanity. The climate crisis is a human rights catastrophe, crushing lives and livelihoods. Its cascading impacts on food security, on migration, on health, on energy, and water threaten human rights now and for generations to come, particularly for women and girls. Meanwhile, digital technologies are widely misused to suppress, limit, and violate our rights through surveillance, online hatred, harmful disinformation, harassment, and built-in discrimination. Artificial intelligence brings new speed and scale to these threats. The splintering of social media platforms into self-selecting channels that cater to their audience contributes to the isolation of individuals, the atomization of societies, and the loss of a shared public space. And in some quarters, human rights are being shunned, vilified, and distorted. This is the backdrop against which my office and the broader human rights ecosystem, including this Council, are working to promote and safeguard the rights of everyone, everywhere. Last year, for example, my office contributed to the release of over 3,000 arbitrarily detained people. We took part in some 11,000 human rights monitoring missions, observed nearly 1,000 trials, and documented some 15,000 situations of human rights violations around the world. In addition to the daily interventions with governments, we issued about 245 statements shining a light on human rights concerns in some 130 countries. Our teams on the ground are supporting countries to improve their laws and institutions and to adopt social and economic policies that reinforce cohesion and address injustice. We contributed to human rights-based approaches to sustainable development, taxation, and public spending from Cambodia to Jordan and Serbia. Support to my office is a low-cost, high-impact investment. I call on you to go the extra mile to make sure that my office, your own national human rights institutions, and human rights non-governmental organizations can continue to do this essential work. Excellencies, since the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, despite setbacks, we have made steady progress. Freedom expanded, particularly for oppressed communities. There was widespread understanding that human rights are the foundation of effective governance, sound economic policies, and social cohesion. Today, we can no longer take that basic understanding and progress for granted. The global consensus on human rights is crumbling under the weight of authoritarians, of strongmen, and oligarchs. By some estimates, autocrats now control around one third of the world's economy, more than double the proportion 30 years ago. Leaders cite national security and the fight against terrorism to justify gross violations. Hypocrisy, double standards, and impunity have also played a part. Regional powers that are neutral or hostile to human rights are growing in influence. Everywhere, we see attempts to ignore, to undermine, and to redefine human rights, and to create a false binary that pits one right against another in a zero-sum game. There are concerted efforts to chip away at gender equality and the rights of migrants, refugees, people with disabilities, and minorities of all kinds. But human rights, from the right to food and adequate housing to the rights to health and education and freedom of speech, are for everyone, and we need an all-out effort by everyone to make sure that human rights and the rule of law remain foundational to communities, societies, and international relations. Otherwise, the picture is very dangerous. In previous centuries, the unrestrained use of force by the powerful, indiscriminate attacks on civilians, population transfers, and child labor were commonplace. Dictators could order atrocity crimes consigning vast numbers of people to their deaths. Be aware, this can happen again, but we are far from powerless to prevent it. Our tools are the United Nations Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the body of international law, and the institutions that work to implement them, including this Council, my office, courts and judiciary, civil society, independent journalists, and human rights defenders around the world. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, today we need an alternative vision. We need the politics of wisdom, rooted in facts, the law, and compassion. First, human rights are about facts. That is why my office is monitoring, documenting, and reporting on violations and abuses in war zones and crises around the world. And I will provide details in my global update next week. In addition to Ukraine and the occupied Palestinian territory, examples include the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Myanmar, Sudan, and Syria, where my office has been documenting abuses and raising the alarm for some for a couple of years, or Afghanistan, where we are reporting on the impact of gender apartheid on women and girls, or Haiti, where my team has reported on the devastating impact of illicit flows of weapons. Never underestimate the power of factual, legal, and moral clarity. Facts on their own can and must prompt action. When the red flags go up, they must trigger an immediate response. That is why the work of this Council and the other human rights mechanisms is so important. While we cannot say exactly how much death and suffering has been prevented by these efforts, we know they make a difference. Second, human rights are about the law, which is a break on power, privilege, and unrestrained profit. Some things are not for sale. Our international legal frameworks and institutions, including the International Criminal Court, are fundamental to ensuring justice and achieving accountability for the most serious of crimes, preventing future violations, and making the world safer for everyone. Equally important are strong institutions at the national level to protect vulnerable people and enable everyone to participate more fully in cultural, religious, social, economic, and public life. It is imperative that we stand up for these institutions when they come under attack. Finally, human rights are nothing without compassion, the glue that unites us in our common humanity. We rarely hear about compassion from today's leaders, but some of the most successful visionaries throughout history, including Nelson Mandela and Eleanor Roosevelt, have led through their remarkable compassion. Human rights go beyond thought leadership to heart leadership. They tap into some of our most cherished ideals of how people should treat each other and the meaning of human dignity. Because of that, they are wildly popular. Human rights have been central to movements for equality and justice throughout history, from the anti-slavery, anti-racism, anti-apartheid struggles to the labor movement, from decolonization to the civil rights movement, the women's movement, marriage equality, and the LGBTIQ+ movement, Black Lives Matter, the indigenous rights movement, the disability rights movement, the climate justice movement, and beyond. Human rights have universal power to move people to action. In countries where human rights are not widely respected, people will risk their lives to defend them. And I want to pay tribute to brave human rights activists and defenders everywhere. This is why even the most repressive governments often use the language of human rights to try to justify themselves. They know that human rights abuses trigger revulsion and reduce their power and influence. Upholding human rights makes eminent sense for stability, for prosperity, for our better for a better common future. Human rights are a winning proposition for humanity, and we will continue to promote, protect, and defend them around the world with humility, determination, and an indomitable hope. Thank you.

President of the Human Rights Council, President of the General Assembly, Secretary-General, High Commissioner for Human Rights, Ministers, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Like every year, it is my great pleasure to welcome you here in Geneva today. But today, I have mixed feelings. On the one hand, I am very proud, and on the other, I am deeply worried. On the one hand, a sense of pride. On 9 October 2024, the UN General Assembly elected Switzerland to the Human Rights Council for the next three years, with 175 votes out of 190. The trust you have placed in my country honours us, and I am very grateful for it. Geneva has also witnessed a historic moment when, by acclamation, our ambassador, Jorg Lauber, was elected 19th President of the Human Rights Council for this year. It is the first time that a senior Swiss diplomat has taken up that office. So that is why I am proud. Let me move on to why I am worried now. Our planet is in a bad state, and as a physician, I cannot ignore that diagnosis. We are living through a time of geopolitical uncertainty, where diplomatic spaces are shrinking, humanitarian crises are multiplying, and the vast majority of the global population is living under authoritarian regimes. We face immense challenges to which we must rise. Here in Geneva, it is our duty to act, and we have the means with which to do so. Ladies and gentlemen, what are the challenges that I speak of? Let's take a look at 2024, last year, a year marked by major elections. More than 4 billion citizens, that's more than half of the global population, went to the ballot box in 76 different countries. That was a genuine test for democracy at the global scale. The result of which is deep unease. Voters expressed genuine distrust vis-a-vis their elected representatives. Young people are becoming more radical, populist parties are gaining ground, and social networks are imposing unfiltered communication upon us. It seems as though the world is losing its bearings. And what are the reasons for this? There are five main reasons I'd like to mention. First of all, Globalization has reduced poverty, but it has left behind it areas of deindustrialization, in particular in the West. Secondly, the digital revolution is shaking up the job market. Thirdly, Identity claims, be they ethnic or sexual identity or other claims, have taken on a scale that is destabilising many societies and many individuals. Fourthly, social networks exacerbate divisions. Fifthly, the climate crisis is fuelling a sense of chaos that is worsening defiance towards people in governance. What can we do? We see that there is a deep crisis of trust, but also we have lost our points of reference. And in this context, human rights are a fundamental bedrock upon which we can stabilize our societies. I'm thinking in particular of individual rights and respect for privacy. the right to free and transparent elections, the right to labour and economic stability, the right to freedom of expression, with the responsibility of the media being recalled, and also the right to a sustainable environment. Nineteen years on from the creation of the Human Rights Council in 2006, one is forced to note that the challenges are growing. The war in Ukraine, and today we mark the third anniversary with a great sense of sorrow, is a tragic example of that. You must also take into account the ongoing tensions in the Balkans, the Caucasus, conflict in the Middle East, instability in Northern Africa, and war in sub-Saharan Africa. The international context is increasingly alarming. While I was preparing this statement for the seventh consecutive year, my optimism gave way to increased realism. I am now convinced that it is more necessary than ever before to focus our efforts on the protection of fundamental rights, especially as regards the right to freedom of expression, of religion and of association, our right to life and to equality before the law, to education, our right to ownership and the total prohibition of torture and slavery. As we face threats against democracies, the Human Rights Council of the United Nations must act united and with determination. The hour is not one for division, but for concerted action in order to uphold the principles that guarantee peace and stability. and that is something that the Swiss presidency can achieve. The primary responsibility of the Swiss presidency is to ensure the smooth running of the Human Rights Council work, thereby enabling it to fully deliver on its mandate. Human rights are not a luxury but a necessity. As our ambassador, Joerg Laubens, said just after he was elected in December 2024, Switzerland is concerned by the decisions of some member states to withdraw somewhat from the council. Human rights are a matter of concern for all of us. Every member of the United Nations should shoulder its responsibilities in this respect. The Swiss presidency is not merely an honour, it is a matter of responsibility. And so I would like to take this opportunity to express my full support for Joaclovan, whose long experience within the United Nations, both in New York and here in Geneva, will serve him well as he seeks to achieve this mission.

Switzerland will continue to carry out with determination the responsibilities it has assumed over the past two years on the United Nations Security Council.

The implication is that the Council's crucial role in addressing abuses, preventing conflict, and its emphasis on the need for peace has become more important. Today, we are witnessing violent conflicts characterized by indiscriminate attacks on civilian populations, including schools, hospitals, use of sexual and gender-based violence as a weapon of war, a rise in violent extremism, dissemination of economic livelihoods, and forced displacements. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, in its Global Appeal 2025, projects that over 139 million people globally will be forcibly displaced or become stateless by the end of 2025 due to conflicts. Most of these are vulnerable people from developing countries. Recent reports by UNICEF indicate nearly 47 million children are displaced due to conflict, with the numbers expected to continue increasing. The global organization Save the Children International reports that one in 11 children are being denied of their basic rights to live, learn, be protected, and prosper due to violent conflict, adverse climate change, and global economic instability. The wars in Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo, Libya, Gaza, Lebanon, Ukraine, Haiti, Myanmar are some of the notable examples of critics' crises, including Africa's forgotten conflicts. They have been spoken to earlier by other speakers. Kenya continues its active engagement in peace initiatives, both regional and internationally, including in DRC, Sudan, Somalia, and Haiti, among others, because we recognize that sustainable peace is linked to the protection and promotion of human rights. We believe the Council's work is more vital than ever before, serving as a critical platform for addressing human rights abuses, which are often both a cause and a consequence of conflict. Mr. President, we believe that despite significant challenges, multilateralism remains our most viable option in addressing global issues and promoting human rights. Therefore, In order to maintain its credibility and effectiveness, we must avoid politicization and selective application of standards. The Council should serve as a platform for constructive dialogue, impartial assessment, and collaborative action, fostering genuine progress in the global human rights landscape. Kenya reaffirms its commitment to advocating for marginalized groups, particularly in the face of rising xenophobia, afrophobia, and racial discrimination. Kenya commends the Council's crucial work in recognizing the inextricable link between climate change and human rights. We acknowledge the urgent need to address environmental crises as a recognition of the direct connection between environmental degradation and human rights abuses. Kenya will continue to champion this cause during our tenure on the Council. In this regard, we emphasize the importance of respecting the principles enshrined in the Paris Agreement We believe that climate finance and the loss and damage fund are critical and represent the bare minimum of what is necessary for a just transition and broader climate justice. We bear witness to the profound impact of climate change in worsening existing vulnerabilities, entrenching marginalization, acting as a threat multiplier, and contributing to instability and conflict in already fragile regions. Mr. President, Kenya recognizes the evolving landscape of human rights challenges in the digital age and is committed to addressing them proactively. We are reviewing our 2014 National Policy and Action Plan on Human Rights to integrate emerging issues, particularly those related to technology and bridging the digital divide. We believe The Council has a crucial role in promoting equitable access to emerging technologies, critical infrastructure, and skills necessary for full participation in the information society. We emphasize that bridging the digital divide is essential to prevent technology from worsening existing inequalities. To this end, during our tenure, Kenya aims to advocate for the recognition of access to technology as an essential component of the right to information as enshrined in Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. We welcome all efforts towards ensuring that technology is accessible, affordable, and beneficial for all. Mr. President, We recognize the right to development as a crucial opportunity to foster an environment where every individual and every society can reach their full potential. Kenya will use its position in the Council to advocate for an equitable and democratic international order to serve all humanity. This includes addressing the critical issue of foreign debt and its impact on states' abilities to promote and protect human rights. We believe the Council is uniquely positioned to provide a platform for discussing and advancing reforms in the global financial architecture to ensure greater equity. Mr. President, Kenya's strong adherence to human rights is evident by its membership in most of the key international human rights instruments, The government remains dedicated to their full and effective implementation, which entails both regular reporting to treaty bodies and constructive engagement in dialogue with them. Additionally, Kenya is an active member of the regional human rights mechanisms, including the East Africa Community Court of Justice and Africa Charter on Human People's Rights. Domestically, Kenya has implemented various legal, policy, judicial, and other mechanisms to safeguard the enjoyment of these rights by all citizens. In 2010, Kenya established one of the most progressive constitutions in history. Its Chapter 4 is dedicated to the Bill of Rights, which protects fundamental freedoms and rights. This Bill of Rights applies to all people and state organs without discrimination. Kenya is cognizant of the fact that corruption is a threat to human rights. Corruption often facilitates and aggravates human rights violations, particularly against vulnerable groups, by hindering the access to rights and services such as legal representation and a fair trial, property rights, education, health, and social protection. We continue to strengthen institutions, legislation, regulations, and policies to fight corruption, including the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission. And in recognition of the valuable contribution of civil society organizations, public and national human rights commissions, Kenya actively engages with them through various fora and incorporates their perspectives in its periodic reports. Kenya has extended the arc of human rights protection to vulnerable groups, including refugees. Through legislation and policies such as the Shirika Plan, which is a premier refugee integration and management program, Kenya has guaranteed the dignity and economic rights of these victims of forced displacement. Mr. President, in conclusion, as a steadfast champion of the Council, and its vital mechanisms, Kenya pledges to continue our proactive engagement on the international stage as we take up our seat in the Council. We reaffirm that human rights remain the cornerstone of our shared humanity, guided by our constitution and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the bedrock of international human rights standards. Kenya is committed to fostering a just society both at home and globally. We have set a high threshold in protecting and expanding freedom of expression, free press, upholding sanctity of life, countering all forms of violence, including gender-based violence and femicide, amongst others. Our cardinal goal is to contribute to a more just, equitable, and a human rights-respecting world for all. I thank you.

President, High Commissioner, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, our world is at a critical juncture. where uncertainty and unpredictability seem to prevail. In addition to widening geopolitical divisions and humanitarian and climate crises, armed conflicts are prolonging unacceptable levels of suffering in many regions. These challenges, which are but some among many, underscore an undeniable truth, namely that peace is needed more than ever. A few years ago, a number of ambassadors asked me about our constant concern for peacekeeping. Since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine and the conflicts that have been ravaging the Middle East and those that continue to scar other regions, our answer has been reaffirmed. Peace as well as efforts seeking to bring peace about, are now at the very top of the world's political and diplomatic concerns. Putting an end to war, President, also involves ending the proliferation of human rights violations that we're seeing. President, if I speak to you today of peace, It is because peace, without any doubt, is the crucial foundation upon which sustainable development and human rights are built. These are the fundamental principles that justify the very existence of this Council, which today is holding its 58th session. Cambodia's experience shows that conflicts can be settled, that transitional justice can be established, and that war zones can be turned into havens of peace, cooperation, and development. However, Cambodia's transformation was not a stroke of luck. The visionary policy of Samdech Techa Hun Sen, our former prime minister, which focused on a win-win approach, sought not only to end decades of conflicts, but also to pave the way for a strategic framework for national reconciliation, stability, and socioeconomic development, which are still going strong today. The results speak for themselves. Life expectancy went from 59 years in 2000 to 76 years of age in 2021. Before the pandemic, our economy boasted an annual average growth rate of more than 7% for over two decades. In 2024, the figure stood at 6%. Last December, our country, along with Senegal, was officially removed from the list of least developed countries. Cambodia was not only successful in its own transition, but our country has also been generous in sharing its lessons learned, and we have made major commitments for global peace. Since 2006, we have deployed around 10,000 blue helmets, including 800 women, in the context of 11 United Nations peacekeeping missions. Our expertise in the area of mine clearance has benefited many regions. President of the Human Rights Council, dignitaries, ministers, members and observers of the Human Rights Council, civil society representatives, and esteemed guests. I thank you, Excellency, and I will now give the floor to His Excellency Wang Yi, member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs, and Minister for Foreign Affairs of China.

President, colleagues, 80 years ago, the United Nations was born amongst the hopes of people around the world to beat swords into plowshares, carrying a lofty dream for all people to enjoy full human rights are marking an important milestone in the course of human progress. 80 years on, global transformation unseen in a century is accelerating, and maintaining peace, promoting development, and protecting human rights are more deeply ingrained convictions. In the meantime, deficits in global peace, development, security, and governance are exacerbating. And we are confronted with the critical question of where humanity is headed in this new era. To answer this question, President Xi Jinping has made a call for the building of a community with a shared future for mankind and put forward the Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative, and Global Civilization Initiative, proposing China's solution to the world. President Xi also points out that promoting and protecting human rights is a common cause for all humanity and necessitates wide consultations and joint efforts. China stands ready to work with all countries to keep to the right approach to human rights and push for the reforms and improvement of global human rights governance. Firstly, we shall stay committed to our original aspiration and founding mission and clarify the true essence of human rights cause. Democracy and freedom are not a decoration for display. The most important yardstick for a country's human rights situation is whether the interests of its people are effectively protected and their sense of fulfillment, happiness, and security improved. Therefore, we need to uphold a people-centered approach, make people's interests the fundamental starting point and ultimate goal, and keep addressing the pressing and practical issues that people care about most. We need to ensure that development is for the people and by the people, its fruits are shared among the people, and its purpose is to deliver happiness to the people. We must say no to any wars and deeds that use human rights as an excuse to interfere in the internal affairs of other countries in disregard of national sovereignty and security and safety of people's lives. Secondly, We should uphold fairness and justice and clarify the goal of human rights cause. As the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states, all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. The two international covenants on human rights clearly stipulate that in no case may a people be deprived of its means of subsistence. Human rights should be an entitlement of all, not the prerogative of a few. The situation of the strong staying strong and the weak staying weak must not be allowed to continue, and the practice of pitting individual human rights against collective human rights must be readdressed. To this end, the rights to subsistence and development should be taken as a fundamental human rights of primary importance, On the premise of safeguarding national sovereignty, security, and dignity, we need to take a balanced approach to individual and collective rights to advance political, economic, social, cultural, environmental, educational, and otherwise in tandem, and to further ensure equality and special protection for specific groups, including women, children, the elderly, and people with disabilities. This is a way to ensure that all types of rights complement and reinforce each other. We must say no to any words or deeds that apply double or even multiple standards on human rights issues. Third, we must stay committed to engagement and mutual learning and clarify the path to promoting human rights. There is no one-size-fits-all model for human rights. Countries choose their own path. to human rights progress according to their national conditions. No path is superior to others, and each has its own distinctive features. Human rights governance should be built by all. The benefits of human rights development should be shared by all. And this path and philosophy should be explored through engagement and mutual learning among all countries. In this regard, it is important for us to uphold true multilateralism, to adhere to the principle of impartiality, objectivity, non-selectivity, and non-politicization, to conduct constructive dialogue and cooperation on the basis of equality and mutual respect, to effectively increase the representation and voice of countries of the Global South, and to build a just, equitable, inclusive global human rights governance system. We must say no to any word and deeds that impose one's own model or will on others and politicize, instrumentalize, or weaponize human rights. President, colleagues, China is further deepening reforms comprehensively to advance Chinese modernization. The modernization we are pursuing is not exclusive. but one of peaceful development, mutually beneficial cooperation, and common prosperity for all countries. China, caring deeply for the future of humanity and the well-being of all countries, will be a practitioner of international cooperation, a promoter of mutual learning among civilizations, and a builder of community with a shared future for mankind. We'll be more proactive in international human rights cooperation and work with all sides together to usher in a better future for the global cause of human rights. I thank you.

Chile has worked in this Council to promote practical alternatives that would make it possible for states to tackle these challenges by reaffirming that security and human rights are not opposing concepts, but rather complementary concepts. Madam Vice-President, Chile's commitment to human rights is reflected in our openness to multilateralism. That is why we have extended an open and standing invitation to the Human Rights Council's special procedures. Since we became a member in 2023, we received five visits of these mechanisms. Furthermore, in 2024, Chile underwent its universal periodic review, and when we did so, we met our commitment Two, establish a national mechanism to follow up on recommendations. We accepted 98.5% of the 329 recommendations we received, and we therefore reaffirmed our conviction that international transparency and scrutiny strengthen human rights protection and democracy. In a world wherein global challenges call for collective responses, Chile supports the work of multilateral bodies. The promise of peace and security, which gave rise to the United Nations after the Second World War, cannot be left aside just because today we have short-term considerations and interests linked to the prevailing situation. To summarize, Chile puts multilateralism at the heart of what we do to protect human rights. We want this forum to continue to be an arena in which there is an effective dialogue, which is committed to the promotion of the protection of the rights of all persons, be these rights civil, political, economic, social, or cultural in nature. Thank you very much for your attention.
I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Chile. And I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Ararat Mirzoyan, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Armenia.

Honourable Chair, ladies and gentlemen, At the outset, I would like to extend my heartfelt congratulations to His Excellency Mr. Jurg Lauber of Switzerland and the whole Bureau of the Human Rights Council on their election. We wish you every success and stand ready to support your important mission. Today, as the world continues to face the consequences of violent conflicts, forced displacement, and gross violations of fundamental rights, the urgency to strengthen the human rights pillar of the United Nations is as relevant as ever. The scale and severity of atrocity crimes and grave violations, as well as our collective inability neither effectively prevent nor ensure accountability, put at risk the whole set of fundamental values upon which the United Nations and its human rights system were created. basic norms on which all and each of us agreed without reservation. Against this background, the role and visibility of the human rights system has increased dramatically. More and more people, civil society organizations and other stakeholders engage with the Human Rights Council, refer to special procedures and treaty body mechanisms. This comes to testify that the human rights pillar remains the inspiration of hope and justice for millions of people, for our citizens. Honourable Chair, I am proud to state that even in most trying times, Armenia continues to make progress in consolidating and strengthening its democratic institutions, enhancing judicial independence, and combating corruption to build a more equal and just society. We have recently established the national mechanism for implementation, reporting, and follow-up of human rights commitments and obligations, and view it as an important domestic mechanism to mainstream rights-based approach in all policy areas. Later this year, Armenia will be presenting its fourth Universal Periodic Review, which has been concluded based on numerous rounds of consultations between governmental and non-governmental organizations, actors. Armenia remains steadfast in its commitment to the protection and promotion of human rights domestically and globally. We strive to provide platforms for diverse voices and find solutions to the most acute issues of human rights and humanitarian domains. In this regard, last year, In December, Armenia hosted the fifth Global Forum Against Crime of Genocide. The forum gathered officials, eminent experts, representatives of international organizations, United Nations Special Procedure mandate holders, civil society, and academia, who looked at the role that small states can play in shaping and moving forward the prevention agenda, examined the evolution of the UN early warning and early response mechanisms, focusing on the necessity to improve operational and policy coherence. Next year, we will have pivotal importance for my country and our commitments to advance global environmental goals as the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the COP17, will be taking place in Armenia. We attach utmost importance to organizing an inclusive Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity. The Armenian presidency will strive to organize a successful conference with full and meaningful participation, including civil society, academia, indigenous people, local communities, women and youth organizations, and other relevant stakeholders. Armenia looks forward to cooperating with the United Nations member states, civil society, and non-governmental organizations in the effective organization of this crucial international environmental conference to bring the global environmental processes back on track for sustainable development and true inclusivity when it comes to multi-stakeholder participation. Ladies and gentlemen, One year ago, in my statement, I made extensive references to the challenges that Armenia was facing. Unfortunately, most of those challenges still remain unresolved, despite the tremendous efforts of my country. Statements coming from our eastern neighbor continue to question the territorial integrity of Armenia. despite the recognition of each other's territorial integrity based on the 1991 Alma-Ata Declaration, which, among others, had reconfirmed that the administrative boundaries of the Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic and the Azerbaijani Soviet Socialist Republic had become international borders between the two independent republics. Moreover, as we speak, The mock trials against 23 Armenian individuals who are arbitrarily detained are taking place in Azerbaijan with disregard of human rights standards for due process. One year ago, The High Commissioner for Human Rights informed this Council that the OHCHR deployed two teams to Armenia to collect information about the situation of more than 115,000 ethnic Armenians from Nagorno-Karabakh. We believe that the results of the mission will be an important contribution towards advancing the reconciliation efforts. The Republic of Armenia. remaining faithful to its agenda on establishment of peace and stability in our region, has made several constructive proposals to the Azerbaijani side, including within the context of the peace agreement, opening of transport infrastructure, mutual arms control and verification mechanism, et cetera, having in mind the necessity to establish a strategic deal that will resolve all major issues. We remain convinced that constructive response and further engagement and demonstration of political will of both parties will largely contribute to opening a new era of peace in our region. In this very context, I would like to once again reconfirm the willingness of the Armenian side to turn the page of enmity and establish institutionalized peace. We are not only ready for this, but will not divert from this path. And I thank you.
I thank the Foreign Minister of Armenia. And I now have the honour to give the floor to Her Excellency Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir. You have the floor, Iceland.

Madam Vice-President, I am tempted to begin my very first address to the Human Rights Council by quoting the preamble of the United Nations Charter, signed eight decades ago this June. To recall the pledge that was made in 1945 in San Francisco, USA, too, and I quote, "Save succeeding generations from the scourge of war and to reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights and the dignity and worth of the human person in the equal rights of men and women and of nations large and small." It seems to me appropriate, as we celebrate the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, to bring these exactly fundamental principles back to our minds, since we regrettably appear to be moving through rather rough seas. The international system is being challenged exactly when we need it the most, with worrying signs of willingness by major states to put aside all of that which has served us so well. Once again, there are those who seek to govern through the rule of the strongest, where might makes right, fundamental human rights be damned, equal rights of nations large and small no longer the guiding principle. The examples of this dangerous trend of disregard for international law are, unfortunately, many. But the clearest sign is something we are very much focused on today, and as we send our best wishes to the people of Ukraine. Today marks the day that the neighbor, Russia, three years ago began its illegal and wholly unjustified full-scale invasion and war of aggression. Slava Ukraini. Distinguished audience, it is my privilege to address this Council as a foreign minister of a country now serving as an elected member. This is the second time Iceland serves on the Council, and we return determined to actively contribute to the Council's core mandate of advancing the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms of all people, and to address human rights violations and abuses anywhere. During our membership, we will focus specifically on children and youth, on the rights of women and girls, and also on the rights of LGBTQIA+ people. there is also ample reason to put exactly these issues front and center. We realize that not every United Nations member state has yet arrived at the same conclusion we have, that advancement of gender equality and human rights of all people, regardless of gender or sexual orientation, is key to releasing the true potential of society. that equality and prosperity are in fact strongly linked. To them I say that we are all God's children, equal and entitled to the same rights and respect. We hope through our work on this Council to bring others further along with persuasion and perseverance. It is a matter of some pride for us that Iceland is seen as a trailblazer in terms of gender equality. While we still have work to do at home, I want to share with you recent development related to political participation and representation, namely that the new three-party coalition government, of which I'm part of, is now led by three women, the first in our history. Iceland has also seen progress with regard to LGBTQIA+ rights. We are now number two on the ILGA Europe rainbow map. We take pride in the policies that underpin this success, and there is broad consensus around them at home. Nevertheless, we are not immune in Iceland to the negative trends that have emerged internationally

backlash against what I consider progress. Ideologies that undermine the existence and rights of individuals, particularly transgender individuals, unfortunately flow now across borders through social media. This is especially concerning as these ideologies now seem to originate in some of the most powerful countries in the world. For me, the starting point is a simple truth: no person should have to live in fear of persecution and violence. This continues to apply if the persecution is based on a person's sexual orientation or gender identity. And we will not hesitate to stand up on their behalf here in this venue, amplifying the voices of those who fight for their rights. Because we are all, we are all born free and equal. Your Excellency, Excellencies, the founders of the United Nations 80 years ago determined to practice tolerance and live together in peace with one another as good neighbors, to unite their strength to maintain international peace and security, and to ensure by acceptance of principles and the institution of methods that armed force shall not be used save in the common interest. Theirs were worthy goals. It would be wrong to say they have all been achieved without difficulties so far. Far from it. The Israeli warfare in Gaza for 15 months following the Hamas terrorist attack on 7 October 2023 is only the latest testament of the failure of our system to address urgent crises. And yet, that complex problem now seems more divisive than ever, the talk of the removal of people from Gaza being only the latest example of the crossroads we now find ourselves at. We also see conflicts elsewhere, where people live in fear and their human rights are being eroded. An example are the rights of women and girls in Afghanistan, which now seem barely to exist. That should not be tolerated in our world. Our international system, the rules-based order we have increasingly lived by, is under attack by forces that mean to reshape our world. who ultimately want to do away with multilateralism altogether. There is only one way to meet these challenges. We must redouble our efforts, recommit ourselves to principles laid out in the UN Charter. It may prove difficult. It may require sacrifices. For sure, it will require sacrifices, since, after all, the world is a different place than it was in 1945, and the United Nations must reflect those changes through reform and renewal. But by addressing, in unison, the challenges faced by humanity, we are more likely to succeed, and only with common rules can we act united. We need to reaffirm our faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of all people, in the equal rights of all people and of nations, large and small. Thank you.
I thank the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Iceland. I have the honor to give the floor to Her Excellency Hana Arayaselassie, Minister of Justice of Ethiopia.

I thank the Minister of Justice of Ethiopia. And I now give the floor to Her Excellency Baiba Braze, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Latvia.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, In the 30 years since the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, we have taken remarkable strides towards gender equality and the empowerment of women. Yet today, We must also confront the stark realities that women and girls face globally. In Afghanistan, Iran, Sudan, the DRC, as progress remains fragile and uneven, women and girls continue to face gender-based discrimination and sexual violence. They are denied access to education and health care and continue to be deprived of fundamental freedoms. We must spare no effort in urgently addressing these challenges. Latvia is an international leader in gender equality and women's representation at the highest positions. Yet, our commitment to women's empowerment is global. Latvia has increased its contributions to the UN Women, other UN bodies to address immediate needs, but also long-term measures to fight inequality and oppression. Together with NGOs, we have implemented projects to rehabilitate survivors of violence in Ukraine and to empower women and girls in Egypt, Ethiopia, Fiji, Namibia, Rwanda, Uzbekistan in the areas of entrepreneurship, digital literacy and STEM. This is our long-term commitment. Mr. President, three years ago, in an act of unprovoked and unjustified aggression, Russia launched a brutal, full-scale invasion of its sovereign, peaceful neighbor, Ukraine. Thousands of innocent civilians have been killed, millions displaced, and entire cities reduced to rubble. There are hundreds of documented and many more unreported cases of Russia's systemic use of sexual violence as a weapon of war. The acts of rape, torture, and humiliation committed by Russian soldiers are cruel and pure evil. Russia's authorities have committed crimes against humanity by using torture as a coordinated state policy towards Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war. Tens of thousands of Ukrainian children have been forcibly kidnapped, illegally deported, and subjected to the so-called re-education efforts, in fact, aimed at erasing their identity. Behind each of those stories lies a broken family, unspeakable pain, and deep scars that persist for generations. Through this campaign, Russia is seeking to deprive Ukraine of its future, and Russia must be held internationally accountable for its crimes. The situation in Gaza and the West Bank, with immense loss of civilian lives, especially those of children and women, is unacceptable. We remain deeply concerned about the health of hostages still in captivity. Further measures to strengthen the protection of civilians and ensure the safe delivery of humanitarian aid at scale is of utmost priority. A negotiated end to all hostilities must be adhered to by all sides. Returning to talks on a sustainable long-term solution is critical to breaking the cycle of violence. Mr. President, Human rights violations are not confined to conflict zones alone. In Russia, the human rights situation continues to deteriorate at an alarming rate. Opposition, human rights defenders, independent media face censorship, imprisonment, and even death. Domestic repression continues to enable external aggression. In Belarus, the recent sham elections were a total farce. The regime continues its relentless crackdown on civil liberties and direct support for Russia's aggression against Ukraine. Over 1,000 political prisoners face cruel and inhuman treatment, long sentences, and mock trials. We will continue to support the Belarusian people and the democratic opposition in their quest for a free, sovereign, and independent Belarus. Mr. President, We all have a stake in the resilience of multilateral system. Latvia stands ready to shoulder greater responsibility in safeguarding the UN Charter and demonstrating global solidarity as a candidate for the UN Security Council for the term 2026-27. We will stand up for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, sustainable peace and stability in the Middle East, engage on the women, peace and security agenda, and address emerging threats in the digital and information sphere. If elected, we will work together for peace and resilience, advocate for the rule of law, human rights, fundamental freedoms, and accountability. I thank you.
Thank you, Excellency. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Mohamed Hassan, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Malaysia.

Mr. President, Excellencies, In this ever-changing landscape, we are facing significant geopolitical challenges, challenges that undermine international peace, security, and the principles of human rights. This is particularly evident in Gaza, where there have been blatant violations of international laws and appalling brutalities. Israel's genocide has led to the unnecessary tragic loss of civilian lives, resulting in profound suffering and devastation. Accountability for human rights violations in Palestine must prevail. As a matter of urgency, Israel must render its cooperation and grant full access to the Commission of Inquiry and Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories. Malaysia also calls for the timely convening of the conference of the high contracting parties to the Fourth Geneva Convention to uphold the General Assembly's resolutions and ICJ rulings. On the humanitarian front, Malaysia reaffirms its support for the reconstruction and disaster relief efforts for Palestinians. We will host the Fourth Ministerial Meeting of East Asian Countries for Palestinian Development, or CEPAD, this year to promote sustainable reconstruction of Gaza and empower the Palestinian community. Excellencies, as the current chair of ASEAN, Malaysia is committed to centering ASEAN's voice on human rights issues through the ASEAN Intergovernmental Commission on Human Rights. On the ongoing conflict and humanitarian crisis in Myanmar, Malaysia aims to create a conducive environment for engagement among stakeholders to rebuild trust, foster inclusive dialogue and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance. The five point consensus remains the bedrock of ASEAN's approach. Malaysia is committed to working closely with the United Nations and its agencies to promote concrete progress and achieve a durable and peaceful resolution to the crisis in Myanmar. To facilitate progress, Malaysia has appointed its ASEAN Special Envoy to Myanmar. We also look forward to strengthening ASEAN engagement in cooperation with the United Nations and human rights mechanisms on human rights issues related to climate change, women and children, health, development and digitalization. We continue to explore capacity building programs to protect vulnerable groups. Excellencies, Malaysia remains committed to promoting and protecting human rights. On the national front, we will continue to prioritize human rights as a fundamental aspect of development and well-being of our people. We demonstrate this commitment by advancing reforms that promote dignity, justice, and equality for all. Malaysia's commitment in advancing human rights is evident through the development of Freedom of Information Act, National Aging Blueprint, National Indigenous People Development Policy, and National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights. We continue to collaborate with the OSCHR through various human rights mechanism. Just last year, we welcome visit by the High Commissioner for Human Rights, the independent expert on the rights of older persons, and the special rapporteur on arbitrary execution. Excellencies, the Human Rights Council should be made more effective by avoiding politicization, application of double standards, and proliferation of agendas. The Council must decisively uphold its mandate to ensure fairness, transparency, and accountability on all human rights violations. To restore trust of the international community and remain relevant, the Council must be responsive to the current global needs and challenges. Malaysia stands ready to contribute to this crucial endeavor. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Malaysia and now call on Her Excellency Imator Faus, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Andorra.

Madame Vice-President, ladies and gentlemen, at this same rostrum just one year ago, we were describing a dark situation in terms of human rights worldwide. The fact is that we have to conclude that, during the last year, which has gone by, worldwide human rights have experienced a setback. The hallmark of last year was the exacerbation of some conflicts, seriously challenging international law. The hallmark of last year was also the new upsurge of a crisis of democratic institutions. Andorra can only express its deep concern about these situations in Ukraine, three-year-old mass invasion, but also in Gaza, Sudan, but also the DRC, which was the subject of a special session of the Human Rights Council in February, without forgetting also the many other conflicts and crises which often, too often, stay in the shadows. And I remember particularly this non-rule of law state, Haiti, in the face of these ongoing and persistent challenges such as the misuse of technology to manipulate information, it is crucial that we strengthen and make more effective the international human rights protection mechanisms, at the front of which we have this Human Rights Council. Gender equality is a concept we have mainstreamed in our public policies, and it is in that spirit that we submitted our report to the Beijing+25 platform. In some parts of the world, there have even been significant setbacks for human rights in this respect. I would like to reiterate our deep concern about the ongoing and systemic violations of the rights of women in Afghanistan and to particularly condemn the exclusion of girls from schools. We are also very attentive to the rights of women in Syria and to the important role they should be playing in the political transition of this country. Thirty years after Beijing took place, our collective efforts will be crucial if we want to ensure that women are fully involved in the building of more inclusive societies. Social inclusion lies also at the heart of Andorra's commitment. Andorra's aspiration is to build a society where diversity is a source of wealth, is a richness, which is why, internationally, we defend multilingualism in the multilateral system. We defend it as a right. Ladies and gentlemen, Extreme poverty, hunger, inequalities continue to undermine social cohesion and sustainable development. At the same time, climate change is making progress and is doing so with devastating consequences. It is jeopardising not only our present, but also the future of the next generations. Before these challenges, we cannot remain indifferent. Today, more than ever, is the time for us to unite our efforts and to act with determination, vision and braveness. We reiterate our unshakeable commitment to continue to work for a more effective and inclusive form of multilateralism, to strengthen values that we continue to consider as being universal values and to guarantee the protection of fundamental rights. ensure that our future is more sustainable, safer and more full of hope than ever. Thank you for your attention. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Andorra. And now I give the honour to give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Abdulatif bin Rashid Al Zayani. Minister for Foreign Affairs of Bahrain.

In the name of God, most compassionate, most merciful. Excellent, Madam Vice President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, may God's peace and blessings be upon you all. It is my pleasure at the outset to salute each and every one of you and to wish your esteemed body success in achieving the lofty ideals and objectives of this council in order to protect and promote human rights as well as the freedoms all over the world. I would like to start by addressing this esteemed council about its commitment to protect human rights in our region, namely the right to life, education -- health, sorry. education, knowledge, and a dignified life. Our achievements in this field are a testimony to our commitment to protecting these rights, namely lofty royal initiatives namely also the royal pardon and amnesty to release more than 3,670 prisoners last year, as well as the successful implementation of the alternative sanctions and open prisons initiative. We are also committed to protecting women and children's rights among a series of initiatives. We are deeply commit, uh, we are, we deeply believe that actions speak much louder than words. In fact, I do not want to delve into the deep and persistent commitment of Bahrain vis-a-vis international obligations. We went under 7 reviews of international conventions and two protocols pertaining to the CRC, CRPD. And I shall not also delve about our success in implementing 128 recommendations out of 172 recommendations of the UPR in the two previous years, as well as our achievement that went beyond expectations when it came to implementing the National Human Rights Plan. Our Preparations are underway for the second part of this journey. All of these initiatives aim at providing the best possible environment for a thriving culture of human rights to all those who live in our beloved Kingdom of Bahrain. In the Kingdom of Bahrain, we are steadfast in our commitment to human rights, the culture of tolerance, peaceful coexistence, and brotherly coexistence. Our dedication to peace is wider than political statements. We are adopting a comprehensive approach. that believes that true development cannot prosper unless we have a stable, peaceful, and sustainable environment, where we respect human rights, where we find the solutions to disagreements through constructive dialogue and compromise rather than through destructive wars. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Our world is facing today global and unprecedented challenges that are compelling us to reiterate our commitment to justice, equality, peace for all the peoples of the world. During the 33rd Arab Summit that was held in the Kingdom of Bahrain under the presidency of His Majesty the King, our Arab leaders reiterated the importance of human rights, of development, of peace. Peace and solidarity, these are the main components for a prosperous future for our peoples. The declaration of the Bahrain summit is a clear vision to promote regional stability and security. It's a call for peace, for equality, and also the need for a greater Arab solidarity for human rights. We are deeply convinced that human rights, development, and peace are closely linked. Our summit called for an international conference to find a solution to the Arab-Israeli conflict that has been lingering for more than 70 years. We have also a series of proposals in the field of human rights, providing health care and education to the victims of regional conflicts. Such initiatives reflect our humanitarian and human commitment to defend human rights, namely those who are victims of these conflicts. We need to work also on promoting the vital sectors that promote resilience and sustainability. Based on our commitment for a real implementation of such initiatives, we have established a national committee that is in charge of coordinating and following up the implementation of the resolutions of the Arab summit. Such a mechanism reflects our respect to fulfill our humanitarian commitments. This reflects our continuous approach to promote human rights, to promote development in the region. We will continue our efforts towards a vision of regional integration, political stability, economic development, and social development for all. It is important to realize that discussions in the field of human rights cannot take place in isolation of some important principles, such as solidarity, peace, and stability. The absence of security, the continuation of armed conflicts are putting the lives of civilians at threat and threatens also the dignity of the human beings. Defending the right to life is the essence of the task of this Council. Bahrain shall remain a strong supporter of regional and international initiatives aiming at protecting and promoting international peace and stability. We are strongly opposed to violence, extremism, terrorism, and intolerance. We call for peaceful solutions to conflicts through diplomatic dialogues. In this context, we reiterate that achieving Lasting and sustainable peace in the Middle East requires the protection of the rights of the human people, to stop its displacement, to establish a fully sovereign Palestinian state that will live in peace with Israel. And we urge the Human Rights Council to orient its efforts towards the achievement of a lasting peace in the Middle East for all the peoples of the Middle East. That's why we call upon your esteemed Council to support the efforts aiming at achieving peace and harmonious coexistence between the peoples of the Middle East. Such a challenge is the main challenge that your Council faces. I am confident that the Council will be up to face, to facing and countering such a challenge. Thank you and may God's peace and blessings be upon you all.
I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bahrain. And I give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Roberto Alvarez Gil, Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic.

Distinguished members of the Human Rights Council, colleagues, representatives of Member States, ladies and gentlemen, it's a profound honor for me to address this assembly during the high level session of the Human Rights Council. On behalf of the government of the Dominican Republic, I'm pleased to reaffirm my to reaffirm our firm commitment to the defence and promotion of human rights worldwide and our determination to continue to contribute actively in this extremely relevant forum, extremely important forum for all of the international community. This Council is an indispensable arena wherein we can consolidate the fundamental principles that promote human dignity, equality and justice. for all peoples worldwide. May I underscore not only the progress made in our nation, but also our ongoing commitment to those values that guide us, which are embodied in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and so many other essential instruments, all of which adopted in the last 80 years of our organization's existence. The Agenda of this high level segment calls us to think about the commitments we undertook in the Beijing Platform, which 30 years on continues to be the cornerstone upon which is built our national policy designed to achieve gender equality and to guarantee the rights of women and girls. In this context, the Dominican Republic has mainstreamed the principles of the plan of action in our public policies and in our foreign affairs policies, driving forward actively the fostering of the participation of women in multilateral bodies by recognising that they are key agents who can consolidate development processes. An example of our firm commitment There, too, is our gender equality law, which has been a crucial tool to make progress in eradicating gender-based violence and eradicating discrimination by ensuring the full participation of women and girls in all aspects of public and private life.
