Mr. President, Excellencies, colleagues, it is a privilege to speak to you today on behalf of the International Development Law Organization. We are meeting at a time when the broad consensus on human rights, which has underpinned the international system since the end of the Second World War, is under tremendous strain. Many speakers have highlighted the alarming and widespread rights violations and conflicts raging around the world. Of great concern also is the growing indifference and mistrust, which is undermining support for human rights in many places. Addressing these challenges will be critical to preserving decades of hard-won progress on human rights. The concept of human rights was revolutionary in large part because of their universality. Eleanor Roosevelt said, Human rights begin in small places, close to home, and unless these rights have meaning there, they have little meaning anywhere. We are seeing the opposite right now. Global surveys have found that while large majorities value human rights as an abstract concept, few feel they're relevant to their own lives. In some quarters, skepticism has taken root, fueled by misperceptions that human rights are impractical, externally imposed, or protect only a select few. And even as memories fade and the world loses the moral clarity of the drafters of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, it is worth remembering their insight that the task of realizing human rights is an enduring one. The declaration begins with the proposition that the recognition of the inherent dignity and of the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the foundation of freedom, justice, and peace in the world. We need to make that argument anew, demonstrating the tangible ways in which rights protect everyone and serve as a bedrock for peace and development. This is recognized in the 2030 Agenda, where human rights and the rule of law are both outcomes and enablers of all the SDGs. Drawing on IDLO's four decades of experience, allow me to share briefly three ways in which strengthening the rule of law is critical in turning rights into reality. First, the rule of law is a powerful force for peace and stability. The most severe human rights violations take place where the rule of law is weak or absent. Effective justice systems help to prevent conflicts by addressing their root causes and resolving disputes before they can spiral into violence. They also play a critical role in laying the foundations for reconciliation, peace and recovery. Second, The rule of law is key to restoring public trust. It helps ensure fairness, accountability and transparency, giving people confidence that institutions are working in the interest of everyone. Tackling corruption and making institutions more accessible and responsive to the rights people care about most are essential. and mechanisms for community involvement that facilitate direct dialogue between people and government, foster an environment of mutual understanding and cooperation. Third, the rule of law can help to accelerate progress on the social and economic rights that are high on people's minds. The rule of law encourages economic growth by providing stability and certainty and enabling fair dispute resolution. It also helps to ensure that development gains are enjoyed in all parts of society by promoting equal economic opportunity. On the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration, we must redouble our efforts to guarantee that women and girls have equal access to the full spectrum of their rights. By ensuring that justice systems protect women's rights, countries can foster economic growth, improve health and education outcomes, and enjoy greater food security. As an international gender champion, this is a personal priority for me. In conclusion, if we are to succeed in addressing today's challenges, we must do more to improve the lives of people. We must be steadfast in the defense of the ideal of human rights, but also in our commitment and effort to make these rights tangible for all people everywhere. And as the High Commissioner said this morning, we must move from thought leadership to heart leadership. Strengthening the rule of law is one of the best investments we can make in our collective future. IDLO looks forward to working with you to build a peaceful, just and sustainable future grounded in the rule of law. Thank you.

We are also seriously taking a lead in ensuring climate justice. and are going to organize a dialogue entitled Sagarmatha Sambad, means the Everest dialogue, on the topic climate change, mountains, and the future of humanity. At the very end, excellencies, I would like to announce our candidacy for the membership of this esteemed council for the term 2027 to 29 and would like to humbly request all eminent members to kindly support our candidacy. Thank you and namaste.
Thank you, excellency. Now, I have the honor to give the floor to his excellency, Mr. Ermar Shaila Salcedo, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Peru.

United Nations Secretary General, President of the Human Rights Council, President of the United Nations General Assembly, High Commissioner for Human Rights, distinguished delegates, we are being faced with a global context which entails very many challenges. We see conflicts in different parts of our world and serious effects of climate change, growing inequality, and increase in violence in different sectors directly affect the enjoyment of human rights of all persons throughout the world. One of the consequences of these multiple crises has been the increase in migration and forced displacement, and Peru has not been able to escape this phenomenon. We are a country where we host migrants and refugees. For this reason, and guided by our traditional vocation of solidarity and abiding by principles, the state of Peru has implemented different policies for the integration and the protection of the rights of migrants and refugees, complying with our international obligations in this respect and, of course, complying with relevant domestic law. However, the sheer extent and size of the situation requires the support of the international community as we undertake these efforts. President, Peru recognizes and values highly the work done by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, and we welcome the fact that the regional office in Venezuela has recently opened again. We very much hope that they are given the necessary resources to ensure that they can fulfil their mandate, including monitoring the situations of persons that are arbitrarily detained in this country, amongst them three Peruvian citizens. As regards my country, Peru has a memorandum of understanding with the Office of the High Commissioner. Different public bodies, as part of this memorandum, receive special technical assistance. and we were delighted to be able to extend the length of this memorandum until 2026. Peru also has a standing open invitation to different universal and regional human rights protection mechanisms. And on our own continent, Peru maintains a constructive dialogue with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. through high-level meetings, the most recent of which was held on 10 February in Washington, DC. President, the State of Peru continues to put in place public policies for the protection and promotion of human rights. In December 2024, we adopted a national multisectoral human rights policy for 2040, which is comprehensive in nature and restates the commitment of Peru to building a society that is fairer, more inclusive and where there is equality. This very month, on the occasion of the week of human rights, the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights has presented a human rights defenders at risk portal, which means that you can now report, monitor and follow up situations that can threaten the life and integrity of those who do such a fundamental job in defending human rights. President, to conclude, I simply wish to restate Peru's commitment to the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, and our support for the work done by the United Nations system as a whole, and more specifically, for the work done by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as the different special procedures and mechanisms for the promotion and protection of human rights that have been approved by this very Council. Thank you.
Thank you. I have the honor to give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Maxim Ryzhenkov, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Belarus. You have the floor, Excellency.

President, colleagues. Let me begin my statement in a way that is highly unusual for a representative of a country which has been branded a million things in the realm of human rights. Today, I will try and explain what life is like in a country where the rule of law has prevailed and thousands of citizens in our country, or thousands of citizens are trying to come to Belarus in order to benefit from our public health services or quality goods. So I will try to explain in full just how absurd any accusations against Belarus are. A country ought to grow more prosperous and more safe. and stronger every year. Tell me, if in a country citizens live under peaceful skies and feel fully safe and not afraid that they're going to be shot or mowed down by a lorry driven by a fanatic, if they do not fear for the lives of their children when they go to school or play in the yard, if they have work and decent wages, enough so that they don't have to save on food, if they have drinking water, heating, electricity, if they use quality organic produce, and if they are politically literate and active, and if there are free kindergartens and free secondary and higher education and free healthcare, can there in such a country be fundamental problems with human rights? That's something we all understand. All of that I've just mentioned are fundamental rights and they include the right to life. And that basically is the picture of Belarus, which we Belarusians know and anybody who's visited Belarus knows as well. And for everyone else, I invite you to visit our country and see it with your own eyes. Of course, everything is not plain sailing in Belarus, but what I have just said is all true. By way of confirmation, you can see that according to the international report on the implementation of the SDGs, Belarus has achieved four goals early: eradicating poverty, ensuring free, clean drinking water and sanitation, reducing inequalities and protecting our ecosystems. So why are people taking to the streets around the world today? We see, watching the BBC and CNN, why they taking to the streets because they're facing problems with their everyday lives. The so-called collective West is gripped with civil disobedience. The participants are not interested in the freedom of the media or nebulous political rights. Peace and security, jobs and wages, pensions and social guarantees, those are the reasons why millions of people are taking to the streets in the old world. Millions of people who have long grown disillusioned with the possibility of resolving their problems through the ballot box or through their governments. In principle, can you possibly hold up as a model the situation regarding political freedoms and the freedom of the media in the old world? There have been major crises recently and Europe is home to crisis where the most fundamental human rights are being violated. And this is something that even in the White House they've come to understand. Most of us, and I'm saying this because of the statements that have preceded mine, understand that the human rights topic is developing not in the right direction. It is acquiring an increasingly contradictory and divisive nature, and we will soon forget what the civilised path for development of these rights is. If you look at the free world, you see how quickly priorities change for the sake of political opportunism. In women's sport, not long ago, people were lavishly handing out Olympic medals to transgender athletes, and today that is considered to be a violation of women's rights. We are once again protecting women from gender extremism. And again, in free Europe, Belarusian and Russian media have been closed down. Our as they say, propaganda from a few channels, could that possibly completely disrupt the media sphere in the West? Just stop it. Even this right of citizens is being violated. People don't even have right to an alternative view. And there is another example of cynicism. The EU prohibits the right to move across borders, not just for its own citizens, but also for the citizens of Belarus and Russia. I'm thinking about Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia, and Finland. We know what they're afraid of. They're afraid of the truth. They're afraid of the truth that their citizens who visit our country might bring with them. What a paradox. 40 years ago, The West introduced sanctions against the USSR for restricting the rights of Soviet citizens to travel abroad so as to prevent them from bringing in the truth of capitalism. Refugees has always been held up as a sacrosanct right in terms of human rights. And today, the Times is writing, the EU is developing a plan to revise the UN Convention on the Status of Refugees. And of course, I'm not even mentioning the climate agenda or human rights related thereto. How can we possibly keep up with such seesawing in human rights? We're tired of so-called developed democracies doing whatever they please while at the same time violating human rights. Belarus has repeatedly warned about the unacceptability of such flip-flop policies. and the invention of dubious human rights notions. When in the West will they finally understand that the UN is to be a platform for dialogue and not one for confrontation? We are prepared to support the UN's leaders in initiatives aimed at ensuring sustainability and justice in international relations, but unless certain countries stop manipulating human rights, nothing can be achieved. Belarus is calling for there to be a global reset in the field of human rights in order to minimise the potential for conflict in human rights, where a diversity of political systems and paths of development and cultural traditions is reflected and where there will be a clear prohibition on any hierarchy in human rights and a clear ban on double standards. Thank you.

Thank you, Excellency. Now I have the honor to give the floor to His Excellency Lord Collins of Highbury, the Parliamentary Under Secretary of State of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. You have the floor, Excellency.

Mr. Vice-President, I stand here not just as a lifelong trade unionist, but also as a minister of an internationalist Labour government, committed to human rights and the rule of law. We have gathered today against the backdrop of an increasingly volatile and uncertain world. Conflicts and geopolitical tensions are robbing people across the world of their most basic rights. That is why the United Kingdom backs Ukraine's right to choose its own future. That is why the ceasefire in Gaza must be fully implemented. We want to see an end to the conflict, with every hostage released and vital aid reaching Gaza. leading to a credible process towards a two-state solution. That's why we welcome the Syrian Interim Authority's efforts to build a more inclusive future for all Syrians. It's why we welcome the Bangladesh engaging with the High Commissioner as it addresses past crimes and future aspirations. It's why we are heartbroken by the suffering in Sudan and commend the DRC for bringing the appalling situation in the east of their country to this Council just two weeks ago. That's why we are urging China to implement the recommendations of the United Nations High Commissioner's Xinjiang assessment and respect the Joint Declaration on Hong Kong. Against this worsening global climate, the United Kingdom is determined to champion equal and inalienable rights for all. So I'm proud that the United Kingdom is standing for election to the Council for the 2026-28 term. Throughout its many terms on the Council, the United Kingdom has always put respect and partnership at the heart of our approach. and we promise to collaborate in the same spirit once again. If elected, we pledge to defend civic space and fundamental freedoms, supporting civil society organisations and human rights defenders. We pledge to champion equal rights for all by standing up for the rights of women and girls and LGBT+ people, whose hard-won rights and freedoms are being so cruelly undermined, and by promoting women's economic empowerment. We will do all we can to uphold the rule of law. Human rights and the rule of law are the basic building blocks of sustainable economic growth, stable societies and humane migration policies. We will prioritise human rights and governance principles, including the use of new technologies and responding to modern slavery. But the United Kingdom is under no illusion that we can do this alone. We cannot. That's why we need your support. And if we have the honour of serving on the Council, we will prioritise practical action to achieve our shared human rights goals and change people's lives for the better. Ultimately, it is only by building genuine, respectful partnerships that we can work together to defend the freedoms we all so hold dear. Thank you.
Thank you, Excellency. Now I have the honor to give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Ziyambi Ziyambi, Minister of Justice, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs of Zimbabwe. You have the floor.

Mr. President, distinguished guests, It is my distinct honor and privilege to address the 58th session of the Human Rights Council. Allow me at the outset to congratulate you on your election as the President of the Human Rights Council. My delegation expresses utmost confidence in your leadership. Mr. President, I am delighted to report that Zimbabwe continues to make significant progress towards the protection and promotion of fundamental human rights. And in that regard, I am pleased to inform the Human Rights Council that on the 31st of December 2024, Zimbabwe enacted the Death Penalty Abolition Act reaffirming our unwavering commitment to the fundamental principles enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. As a nation, we recognize that the right to life constitutes the cornerstone of all human rights, as articulated in Article 3 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 6 of the ICCPR. The abolition of the death penalty represents a historic milestone in Zimbabwe's efforts towards consolidating a justice system founded on human dignity, equity, and respect for the sanctity of human life. The Death Penalty Abolition Act clearly attests to Zimbabwe's dedication and commitment to aligning its national legislation with international human rights standards and obligations. The Act amends several existing statutes to eliminate any provisions concerning the death penalty, substituting them with the principles of rehabilitation, proportionality and justice. The Act also introduces transitional provisions to guarantee that individuals previously sentenced to death are re-sentenced in accordance with ideals of fairness and human dignity. Mr. President, Zimbabwe has taken significant strides towards enhancing access to justice through decentralising courts and legal aid directorates, to districts and the introduction of a performance management system for the judiciary to enhance efficiency and effectiveness. Equally important and mutually reinforcing is the integrated electronic case management system that was rolled out in superior courts and is now being cascaded to lower courts. Mr. President, Zimbabwe has been grappling with unprecedented climate changes due to recurrent El Nino-induced droughts, which have placed considerable strain on our economy. To mitigate climate change, Zimbabwe is implementing the Presidential Climate Proof Agricultural Production Scheme, prioritizing mechanization and irrigation using existing water bodies. As a result, we have achieved self-sufficiency in wheat production. Other schemes on food security include programs such as the Food Deficit Mitigation Program and the School Feeding Program. In this regard, we acknowledge support rendered by development partners. In recognition of these people-centered, transformative agricultural policies, Zimbabwe won the prestigious 2024 Africa Food Prize as an acknowledgment of Zimbabwe's commitment to sustainable development, food security, and nutrition. Mr. President, Zimbabwe's chairmanship of SADC exemplifies the collaborative spirit of our people and the strong partnerships that we have continued to foster regionally and globally. As we continue to address our human rights obligations, We are determined to ensure that our legal framework and processes respect both domestic, regional and international standards. As part of our commitment to, and in compliance with, human rights obligations and mechanisms, my Government continues to cooperate with special mandate holders and endeavours to be up to date with its reporting obligations, with various reports due for review this calendar year, such as the periodic report to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, due for consideration on 6 and 7 March 2025. Further, my government is ready to host the working group on violence against women and girls, its causes and consequences in August 2025. Mr. President, Zimbabwe's economy has continued to be negatively impacted by the illegal and unilateral coercive measures imposed by some powerful Western nations. The UCMs have negatively impacted the realization of fundamental human rights by ordinary Zimbabweans and vulnerable groups. These UCMs are in violation of the UN Charter. We are therefore strongly denouncing them and call for their immediate and unconditional lifting. In conclusion, Mr. President, Zimbabwe remains steadfast in its pursuit of human rights justice and sustainable development of all its people. In unity, we can overcome adversity and emerge stronger. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you, Excellency. Now I have the honor to give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Damas Nabarro, Minister for Constitutional and Legal Affairs of the United Republic of Tanzania. You have the floor, Excellency.

Mr. Vice President, distinguished members of the Council, Excellencies, dignitaries, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor for me to address this high-level segment of 58th session of the Human Rights Council, especially when our Excellency, Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of United Republic of Tanzania prioritizes the promotion and protection of human rights, which has been placed at the forefront of the government business. This is in recognition of the government's role as the main duty bearer in promoting and protecting human rights. I begin by extending my congratulations to you, Ambassador, Jorg Berger, for being elected President of the Council in 2025. I assure you of my delegation's full support as you steer this august Assembly in the important work of promoting and protecting human rights across the globe. Mr. President, the Constitution of the United Republic of Tanzania and the Constitution of Zanzibar uphold human dignity and the spirit of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The government implements a human rights-based approach to development, hinged on fundamental principles of equality and non-discrimination. This resonates with the governance strategy adopted by Her Excellency, the President of the Republic of Tanzania, which is based on the four RRR principles, being reconciliation, resilience, reforms, and rebuilding. To achieve these principles, candid discussions, participations, engagements, and meetings are held in appreciation of diverse views. This has been the government approach in addressing and mitigating potential challenges which can inadvertently affect civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights of Tanzanians. Mr. Vice President, this is the approach that the government is using to address challenges in the Ngorongoro Conservation Area where there's a need to balance human rights and livelihood on one side and conservation on the other. Her Excellency, the President, personally met with the local and traditional leaders of the area, listened to their concerns, and established two advisory committees launched on 20th of February of this year. The objective of the first committee is to advise on the land matters in the area, and the second committee is to advise on the ongoing voluntary relocation programme of residents from Ngorongoro to Msomera. The objective is to ensure that voluntary exercise operates smoothly and that the concerns of the people are addressed. The principle of participation through continuous engagement and consultations has been instrumental in maintaining stability in this area. Mr. Vice President, on civil and political rights, the country is preparing to hold the general election October this year. We have traditionally are the free and fair election every five years where people have exercised their democratic rights through votes as provided by the constitutions and in total compliance with international and the regional human rights treaties we have ratified. Local government elections held on 27 November 2024 where all 19 registered political parties participated. Mr. Vice President, media pluralism continues to flourish in the United Republic of Tanzania to ensure that people enjoy their rights to freedom of expression and access to information. In mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar, there are currently 351 newspapers, 427 magazines, 245 radio stations, 82 television stations, eight online radio, 400 online televisions, 123 online blogs, and 10 online forums. Mr. Vice President, when it comes to promoting and protecting the right of vulnerable groups, the government is determined to ensure that people with disability are not left out of the development agenda. On the 4th December 2024, the government launched a national action plan on the rights and welfare of people with albinism, as well as the national assistive technology strategy for people with disabilities. These two strategies represent government commitment to the breaking down barriers, creating opportunities, and ensuring that every Tanzanian, regardless of disability, can live a life of dignity and contribute meaningfully to the society. Mr. Vice President, with respect to the socioeconomic rights, headway is being made in bringing closer services to the people. Access to water is currently at 80%, and the rural electrification project has resulted in 96% availability of electricity in rural areas. There has been great progress in the health sector, where maternal health and infant mortality rate has been well addressed. Maternal death per 100,000 births have reduced by 80% in the past seven years, the period which has witnessed a one-third reduction in under-five mortality rates. These transformative gains on the right to life are a testament of Tanzania's comprehensive approach to maternal, newborn, and child health. Mr. Vice President, In Tanzania and many other parts of Africa, where the impact of climate change related challenges have significantly affected the lives of women, it is crucial that government recognize the right in a clean and safe environment. It is for this reason that our excellence, Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, the President of United Republic of Tanzania, has been championing the use of clean cooking energy and encouraging women to stop using charcoal, as it is women and girls who are the most affected by this charcoal and firewood as a source of energy for cooking. Mr. Vice-President, the United Republic of Tanzania is a staunch believer that the promotion and protection

Human rights cannot be achieved in isolation. Therefore, the government works with development partners, civil society, and other actors who share a common vision to ensure that men, women, and the children of the United Republic of Tanzania enjoy the benefits from their human rights and fundamental freedom. Mr. Vice President, thank you very much.
Thank you, Excellency. Now I have the honor to give the floor to His Excellency, M. Mohamed Ali Nafti, Minister for Foreign Affairs and Migration and Tunisians Living Abroad of Tunisia.

In the name of God, the merciful, President of the Human Rights Council, Tunisia has ratified most of the United Nations conventions and we are home to the office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. We also welcome special procedure mandate holders. We are committed to ensuring human rights at the political, national, socio-economic and cultural levels. We would like to reaffirm our commitment to the various initiatives aimed at protecting human rights and to doing so through the UN and at the regional level. We have submitted a report to the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination after having submitted national reports over the past few years to the Universal Periodic Review, the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women and the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. President, my country is firmly set on the path of reform, which began in 2021. The purpose is to promote democracy, enshrine the rule of law, ensure good governance, and also to guarantee the rights and freedoms of all Tunisians without any exception, be it at the legislative or practical levels. We ensure that all elections reflect the will of the Tunisian people and that elections are held in respect for integrity and transparency. We are firmly committed to the fact that rights are indivisible. There are no differences in hierarchy between rights and freedoms, and we seek to promote economic, social, cultural rights in order to ensure decent standards of living for all of our society and in all of its aspects. Human rights are intrinsically linked to social justice, and our state is trying to combat subcontracting in our society, for this is a way of hiding human trafficking and slavery. We seek to ensure that all development processes are human-centred. Illegal migrants are the victims of the global system, and Tunisia is a victim as well, in a sense. We are trying to address this issue by upholding our laws and international law and by ensuring that the dignity of trafficked persons is ensured. We need to dismantle criminal networks that thrive on regional crises and socioeconomic precarity. We are adopting an approach of joint and proportionate responsibility in order to try and find solutions. My country rejects all desperate attempts to impose projects for settling illegal migrants and attempts to exploit this issue in the media or for political purposes. We object to the suffering of migrants being exploited in this way. Despite the efforts that we have made through our justice system and our diplomacy, more than 10 years have elapsed since corrupt regimes fell in our country. We would like to reiterate our call to the members of this Council to support us as regards to recovering looted funds. It is important to support the project of the African network that was adopted by the African Union on the negative impact of the non-recovery of unlawful gains. These gains need to be sent back to the country of origin. Recovering such funds is a fundamental right that is enshrined in international law, including the UN Convention on Combating Corruption. many developing countries have had to resort to foreign debt and cannot recover their funds that have been plundered abroad. Regarding the international financial system, we need to try and reduce levels of foreign debt and the cost of servicing that debt for developing countries. President, we commend the idea of achieving a cease, we commend a ceasefire in Gaza and it is important to prosecute the perpetrators of crimes and war crimes including genocide against the Palestinian people, our brotherly people. We are firmly opposed to the displacement of the Palestinian people which should be able to enjoy its right to live in Palestine and create its own state with Jerusalem as capital. Thank you.
Now, I have the honor to give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Elnoor Mammadov, Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan. You have the floor, Excellency.

Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. It is my honor to address the high-level segment of the 58th session of the Human Rights Council. We send our congratulations to His Excellency Ambassador Uur Glauber on his election as a president of the Human Rights Council and wish the newly elected Bureau continued success in all endeavors. Today, the world confronts multiple crises, including ravaging conflicts, climate change, deepening inequalities, erosion of multilateralism, growing disregard for the fundamental norms and principles of international law, which endanger enjoyment of human rights and fulfillment of basic human needs in every part of the world. It is precisely the time when we have to demonstrate international solidarity and cooperation, step up our efforts to build more effective multilateralism, strengthening the United Nations as a central multilateral system. Azerbaijan is actively engaged in cooperation within the human rights framework, including treaty bodies and special procedure mandate holders. Most recently, our periodic reports under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhumane, and Degrading Treatment or Punishment have been reviewed. Excellencies, climate change is one of the greatest challenges of our time with adverse impacts that are increasingly felt by all, particularly by the vulnerable communities. We need to strengthen our collective actions to address the climate change and accelerate meeting our obligations under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement. In this regard, the 29th Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, successfully organized in Baku, was significant in demonstrating Azerbaijan's leadership at the international level. Under the presidency of Azerbaijan, the COP29 successfully realized two key priorities. First, the new collective quantified goal on climate finance, NCQG, and second, the implementation of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement for carbon markets. Along with many other tangible outcomes, the NCQG decision adopted at COP29 for the first time in the history of climate negotiations included a call for all actors to increase climate funding to developing countries from all public and private sources to 1.3 trillion United States dollars annually by year 2035. 14 global and seven regional initiatives announced as part of the COP29 Presidency Action Agenda receive support at the global level and aim to strengthen climate action. Excellencies, the end of the long-lasting armed conflict with Armenia and restoration of Azerbaijan's sovereignty and territorial integrity have opened enormous prospects for bringing peace and stability to our region, turning the page of enmity and embarking on good neighborly relations. Despite the wounds of the armed aggression imposed on my country, the wisdom of our nation has enabled us to offer peace to Armenia. Over the past year, Azerbaijan and Armenia have registered a significant progress in the normalization process through direct bilateral negotiations, in particular with respect to drafting a bilateral peace agreement and the delimitation and demarcation of the state border. At this point, we expect Armenia to eliminate the key barrier in the normalization process, which is to legally abandon territorial claims against Azerbaijan through the constitutional amendments. The post-conflict rehabilitation requires eradication of all consequences of the conflict, which includes, in particular, bringing suspected perpetrators of atrocious crimes to justice. This is not only the right, but the obligation of Azerbaijan under international law to hold to account those suspected of having committed war crimes. This is the context within which the trials currently undertaken in Azerbaijan, which the Foreign Minister of Armenia mentioned today, should be viewed. We have ensured and will continue to ensure all the procedural rights of those accused in accordance with the international standards of due process, but justice will be served. Speaking of the crimes committed during the war, it is of vital importance to shed light on the fate of about 4,000 citizens of Azerbaijan who went missing as a result of the conflict and to end the continuing suffering of their families. We call on the relevant UN bodies and mechanisms to keep this issue high on the agenda and demand full cooperation from Armenia in order to bring clarity to the fate and whereabouts of our compatriots. Another pressing issue is to ensure safe and dignified return of more than 250,000 Azerbaijanis expelled from Ar- Armenia during the early years of the conflict, who remain deprived of the an- ancestral homeland in blatant violation of international human rights law. The calls of Western Azerbaijan community, once constituting the largest national minority in Armenia, to start a dialogue on facilitation of the peaceful return remain disregarded and often deliberately misinterpreted by the Armenian government as a territorial claim by Azerbaijan. This is an issue of concern for us that require due consideration by the relevant UN mechanisms. It is noteworthy that Azerbaijan has engaged in large scale post conflict reconstruction efforts for ensuring the right of 100,000 of internal displaced Azerbaijanis to safe and dignified return to the formerly occupied territories. Azerbaijan has developed and implemented the program of great return as a result of which several hundred families. have already returned to their homeland. Regrettably, the massive contamination of territories of Azerbaijan with landmines and other explosive devices remains a significant obstacle to the smooth progress of our reconstruction efforts. Since the end of the conflict in 2020, up to 400 individuals, mostly the civilians, have fallen victim to landmines. With this in mind, Azerbaijan has introduced a national goal, SDG 18, focusing on the mine action. We are thankful to all stakeholders who have contributed to humanitarian demining in Azerbaijan. And given the scale of the problem, we reiterate our call for increased international support to strengthen Azerbaijan's humanitarian mine action capacity. We also call on the Council and the relevant special procedure mandate holders to address the negative impact of mines on enjoyment of human rights and the rehabilitation of mine victims. In conclusion, I wish to reaffirm our commitment to contributing to international peace and security, promoting respect for international law and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms for better future for all. And I thank you.

Thank you, Excellency. Now I have the honor to give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Remy N'Goye Lumbu. Chairperson of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights of the African Union. You have the floor, Excellency.

Thank you. President of the Human Rights Council, High Commissioner for Human Rights, distinguished participants, all other protocol observed. Allow me at the outset to congratulate you on how you have been leading our debates today, and allow me to congratulate you on your election and to assure you that the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights will stand by you and support you throughout your mandate in the framework of cooperation that we hope is mutually beneficial. My name is Remy Nguimbou, I'm the President of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights and Special Rapporteur on Human Rights Defenders in Africa and a focal point on reprisals and focal point on judicial independence in Africa. Yesterday, the preparatory work for the International Charter on Human Rights through its three major pillars, first, and then the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the International Covenant on Economic and Social Rights, and then through all subsequent extensions to those and additional conventions, brought promise of great hope for humanity. The question now is, Does that hope still hold true with those that work today? The efforts to implement the very same charter, in the name of which this 58th session of the Human Rights Council has been opened, do not bear the same promise as in the past. What can be done? In the meantime, an African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights was born in 1981. It entered into force in 1986. Its ambition was to pinpoint hallmarks of Africa which ought now to be taken into account. The particularity of this charter is that the individual focused approach to human rights is possible in Africa only in a community context or a more comprehensive global context without it being necessary to point the finger in the event of violation and in order to foster dialogue. That is what we call in Africa Ubuntu Sophia or Ubuntu philosophy of human rights. The African Commission on Human and People's Rights is the oldest body of the African Union and it is the first regional institutions have been tasked with the protection and promotion of human rights and the rights of peoples in Africa. It is the body of the African Union that is the closest to our citizens because it is accessible to everyone through its quasi-judicial framework that is flexible and people-centered. The vision of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights in accordance with our with our charter, the African Charter, is to foster human rights and to interpret the provisions of the Charter. In accordance with our mandate for promotion of human rights, the ACHPR has carried out more than 90 promotion exercises and we have devised seven additional draft protocols to the African Charter, six of which have already been adopted by the African Union, and we have also developed over 35 non-legally binding instruments in order to clarify the provisions of the African Charter so as to facilitate its implementation. Regarding the mandate for protecting human rights, To date, the African Commission on Human People's Rights has been seized with more than 862 communications, four of which are interstate ones. We have also been working on We also submit periodic reports that are submitted to us by the States regarding the implementation of our Charter and its protocols, following which we provide concluding observations which take note of progress and areas of concern, and we make recommendations. The exercise to which African States submit themselves in this way is very, very similar to the treaty body reporting system, but unfortunately we do have problems with delays. Many states are behind in submitting their reports in Africa to the African Commission, even though they are usually here before the Human Rights Council for the Universal Periodic Review. So our recommendation would be that such regular presence within the UPR ought to be reflected at the level of the reviews before the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights. Our commission has created special mechanisms that are akin to the special procedures in order to fully deliver on its mandate, but we work very closely with many UN special procedures. Regarding how my body cooperates with other institutions that are tasked with achieving the same mandate, I can tell you that it is with pleasure that our Commission very recently hosted the joint framework for the African Union and the United Nations on human rights, which was signed by the UN Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres, and the President of the Commission of the African Union, His Excellency Moussa Faki Mahamat. That said, we have also built bridges for cooperation with all national human rights institutions in Africa and with civil society organisations. In fact, we are the institution that collaborates the most with civil society organisations and which gives them pride of place during our sessions. To date, the Commission has granted the status of affiliate to 37 national human rights institutions including two specialized institutions, and we have granted observer status to 579 NGOs. And yet we do face several challenges within the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, and one challenge relates to funding. And here I would like to appeal to you all because if, unless things change, there will be no more Human Rights Commission in Africa because the amount of funding available is ever dwindling. Allow me, before concluding, to highlight a few steps forward that have been achieved in Africa, and then I will also pinpoint a number of areas of concern. Regarding the positive aspects, the Agenda 2063 defined the great aspirations we harbor for the Africa we want, with an implementation monitoring plan as well. We've created the continental free trade area, and recently, protocols to the African Charter on the Protection of the Rights of Older Persons and a protocol on the rights of persons with disabilities have entered into force. We have also adopted regional human rights protection instruments, the most recent of which was the adoption during the 38th session of the African Union General Assembly of a new convention of the African Union on the elimination of violence against women and girls. This is in the context of our African positive masculinity. I'd also like to inform you that there is a trend of moving towards abolishing the death penalty in Africa, and their states are complying with the moratorium on executions for the most part. I would also like to talk about the charity-based regime that governs human rights in Africa. Africa always has to have its hand outstretched in order to get attention, be that here or in other fora or before the 54 states of our African continent. The fact that Africa has to abide by this charity-based regime is something that you all ought to pay attention to. I'd also like to say that the sound of marching boots and weapons continues to deteriorate our security situation with multiple repercussions on human rights. In particular, we have persistent armed conflicts For instance, in the east of the DRC, conflicts which have been condemned by resolution 2773 of the United Nations Security Council. And the African Commission would like to draw member states' attention to this resolution so that it might be implemented and serve to alleviate the suffering of citizens in that region. I'd like to draw your attention to Sudan, where an unprecedented humanitarian disaster is underway. My institution is currently carrying out a fact-finding mission. I must also mention what is happening in Somalia, what is happening in Ethiopia in the Amhara region. Allow me also to draw your attention to the persistence of terrorism in North Cameroon, which is having a major impact on citizens. This also warrants your attention and your support. All these countries are suffering either from war or from terrorism. Allow me also to mention the Sahel region and instability in the Mozambique Channel. Allow me also to share with you another cause for concern, for Africa, and that is political instability that stems from anti-constitutional coups, which are prohibited, categorically so, by the African Charter on Elections, Democracy and Good Governance. I'll mention the three countries that you'll be familiar with already, Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso. Even though these countries have been suspended from the African Union as regards their right to participate in certain bodies, our commission, the African Commission on Human Rights and People's Rights, continues to interact with these three countries, because you cannot suspend human rights. In fact, Burkina Faso even submitted a periodic report during one of our sessions, and we made recommendations for the benefit of the citizens of Burkina Faso. Before concluding, I'd also like to speak to you of another source of concern in the domain of economic, social and cultural rights, and that is youth unemployment. Young people aged under 25 represent 60% of our population, and there are no jobs for young people in Africa, so this is an appeal that I'm making to African states to tackle that problem. Also, basic infrastructure is in short supply or inadequate. Schools, hospitals, there are not enough of them in Africa. I'd also like to mention exploitation and the inequitable distribution of resources, corruption and its impact on the development of many of our countries. By way of conclusion, President, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights remains committed to cooperating with all stakeholders in order to strengthen protection and promotion of human rights in Africa. We call for concerted action, inclusive action and sustained action in order to advance the rights of African people. Thank you.

Thank you, Excellency. Excellencies, distinguished participants, this was the last dignitary we could accommodate at this meeting at this point. Your Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, we will now begin our annual high-level panel discussion. Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for the opportunity to join you today. My sincere thanks go to His Excellency, Duke Labr, President of the Human Rights Council, for the kind invitation to address this annual high-level panel. This year, we commemorate the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action adopted at the Fourth World Conference on Women. This should ideally be a moment to celebrate 30 years of progress, yet we are forced to confront hard truths. The truth is so stubborn that it is irreversible and eternal. While there has been some progress in areas such as closing the gap on girls' education, improving health outcomes for women, and the adoption of more gender-related laws, we are still a long way off from achieving gender equality and women empowerment. We have a moral obligation to promote the empowerment of women all the time and everywhere. Globally, women's rights are under threat or being curtailed outright, reversing years of hard-won progress. Concurrently, fewer resources are being devoted to support initiatives aimed at advancing gender equality. This affects women's education, health, and the ability to participate in politics. It also hurts their decision-making as concerns matters of economic opportunities. Sometimes we forget that women's rights are fundamental human rights. In many societies, the fundamental freedoms of movement, association, and speech of women continue to be restrained in various forms. Such restrictions are socially unnecessary and discriminatory. Today's commemoration is therefore both timely and urgent. It is a commemoration which celebrates the past, the present, and the future. We must act with greater resolve to uphold the Beijing Platform for Action in both word and deed, and strive with renewed determination to protect the rights of women and girls. Excellencies, we would be remiss if we did not recognize successes and areas to build upon. Today, more countries than ever before have adopted laws to advance gender equality, including to protect women and girls from violence and ensure non-discrimination. Governments have adopted numerous policies and programs to address education and training, social protection and economic empowerment targeted at women and girls. Women and girls occupy a place of choice in my presidency of the United Nations General Assembly. In legislatures globally, the share of women parliamentarians has grown from 11 to 27 percent. While this is far from parity, it nevertheless constitutes a good step in our onward march towards gender equality and the empowerment of women. We have the opportunity now to seize that momentum. In September last year, Member States reaffirmed their commitment to accelerate efforts to promote women's rights and achieve gender equality in the Pact for the Future. The Pact affirms that this is essential to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Through implementation of the Pact for the Future, we can address the obstacles that are holding back our progress. There are some examples. First, such as the sad reality that women and girls continue to be more harmfully impacted by conflict and wars. Secondly, that 736 million women have experienced physical, and/or sexual violence at least once in their lives. Third, that an additional 158 million women and girls will be pushed into poverty by 2050 if the current climate change statistics are not reversed. And fourth, that the digital divide is more pronounced along gender lines with a 19% gap. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, a few days ago, I was designated as an international gender champion. This was not meant as an award, but rather as a call to duty. All of us, particularly those of us in positions of authority, have a responsibility to champion gender equality in all our activities. We have a responsibility to empower women and girls at every step. It is a responsibility that I take very seriously, and I have reestablished the Advisory Board on Gender Equality to guide me in these efforts. The Board will help to ensure that gender equality is integrated in the high-level events and work of the General Assembly from non-communicable diseases to social development, from youth to artificial intelligence. The Board will also guide my efforts in planning the commemoration of the anniversary of two important milestones in the global agenda for gender equality. First, the 30th anniversary of the Fourth World Conference on Women, which will be commemorated with a high-level meeting in September 2025. And secondly, the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the UN Security Council Resolution 1325, which will offer an opportunity to reaffirm our commitment to increase the participation of women in the prevention and resolution of conflicts and incorporate gender perspectives in all United Nations peace and security efforts. Excellencies, gender equality is a moral imperative that is essential to humanity's collective progress. The Pact for the Future and the Declaration on Future Generations demand the full implementation of international commitments on women's rights. The 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration and platform for action must be more than a commemoration. It must be a call to action for the advancement of the rights of every woman, everywhere. We must reaffirm our commitment urgently and unequivocally to its full realization. Let this anniversary be a moment of resolve, a turning point where we choose action over rhetoric, commitment over complacency. Thank.
