Thank you very much. It is now an honor for me to give the floor to Mr. Volker Tur, United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. Your Excellency, you have the floor.

President of the General Assembly, distinguished panelists, very happy to be here on this very important occasion to discuss the mainstreaming of gender equality. The Beijing Declaration and Platform of Action was a milestone in the history of women's rights and gender equality, and I know that many of you have actually actively participated in it. It encapsulated the incredible mobilization, the wisdom and expertise of feminist movements and women's rights organization, and it led to major progress. The declaration sparked a global stand against gender-based violence. More than 160 countries passed laws to address domestic violence. The number of women in parliaments around the world has more than doubled since the declaration, and 50 million more girls have been enrolled in schools globally since 2015. We urgently need that same mobilization and solidarity today. to counter a growing backlash against women's rights and gender equality, especially targeting sexual and reproductive health and rights. We need to rally around the declaration and the platform for action to send a clear message that resurgent gender-based violence, discrimination, and misogyny have no place in our world. Excellencies, distinguished Delegates, violence against women is a persistent scourge, and it's rampant online, on our streets, and in our homes. Six women or girls are killed every single hour by their intimate partner or family member, and the real numbers are most certainly higher. In 2023, the proportion of women killed in armed conflict doubled compared to the previous years. and the number of United Nations verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence grew by 50%. The outdated notion that men should control women's choices and bodies is gaining traction once again. Even the very concept of gender equality is being questioned. It is shocking and bewildering to me that misogynist influencers have millions of followers on social media and are hailed as heroes in some quarters. Women's rights are being dismissed and denied in one form or another all over the world. Not one country has achieved gender equality. This is a massive human rights failure and a problem not only for women and girls, but for everyone. No country can make sustainable progress politically, economically, or socially while subordinating or excluding half of its population. Women's full leadership and participation make peace agreements more durable, development more sustainable, climate action more effective, and economies more resilient. Take the climate catastrophe. Women and children are 14 times more likely than men to die in extreme weather events And four out of five people displaced by climate change are women and girls. No region can truly address the climate crisis without listening to women, who are uniquely positioned to be agents of change. Take diplomacy, where a growing number of countries have adopted a feminist foreign policy over the past decade. They are prioritizing equality and justice as preconditions for peace, prosperity, development, and security. This recognizes, for example, that women's participation increases the probability of a peace agreement lasting 15 years by at least 35%. Or take economic growth. Estimates suggest that closing the gender pay gap could give the global economy a 7 trillion US dollar boost. Women's rights and gender equality are non-negotiable. They will have an outsized, catalytic, and multiplier effect across all the sustainable development goals. We know that progress is possible. Our history and the leaders of the women's rights movements can show us the way. So too can the women and girls all over the world who are demanding an equal share. My office is working with them to advance their struggle. In Mexico, we are backing the fight against impunity in cases of femicide. In Colombia, we supported key peacebuilding activities with women at their core. We are working to increase the participation of women in decision-making in South Sudan. And in Ukraine, we are supporting women survivors of conflict-related sexual violence. We will continue to support efforts like these all over the world, celebrating diversity, insisting on bodily autonomy, pushing for equality in family spaces, in culture, and in religion, and pressing for more women at decision-making tables. We will promote and protect women's rights and gender equality every day at every opportunity, in my office's advocacy and in my engagement with states. This is my firm commitment. to women and girls in all their diversity everywhere. But this also needs to be a national priority and a global commitment, a promise by states and societies to women and girls to stand up for their rights, to protect and develop the legacy of the Beijing Declaration, and to dismantle the patriarchy brick by brick. Thank you.
Thank you very much. Thank you. I would now like to invite Sima Bahous, Executive Director of UN Women, to deliver a video message.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor to join you in commemorating the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action. 30 years ago, the world made a promise to advance the rights, opportunities, and dignity of all women and girls. That promise was not just words on paper. It was a blueprint, a rallying cry. And for three decades, it has fueled progress. More girls in school, more women in parliaments, more laws protecting women from violence, more nations recognizing gender equality as a necessity. But let us be honest, we are not where we should be. Women and girls' rights are under attack. The spaces for women's voices are shrinking. And if we continue at this pace, a girl born today will be 39 years old before women hold as many seats in parliament as men. She will be 68 before child marriage ends, and she will be 137 years before extreme poverty for women and girls is eradicated. We cannot accept this. This year's Commission on the Status of Women is a moment to act decisively, invest ambitiously, and demand accountability. A moment to push for a bold, forward-looking political declaration that does not just reaffirm commitments, but accelerates them. We cannot do this alone. Change has always been contested, and our response must be just as strong. We must build alliances, amplify voices, and stand firm, including here in the Human Rights Council. Excellencies, the Beijing Platform laid the foundation for a world where all women and girls have equal rights and opportunities. Now, at Beijing+30, we need an all-hands-on-deck approach to turn that vision into reality. Our review of progress from 159 member states points to six urgent priorities. close the digital gender gap. Ensure every woman and girl can access technology and shape the future. End women's poverty, not in a century or a generation, but in our lifetime. Stop violence against women and girls. Pass and enforce laws and dismantle the norms that allow violence to persist. Ensure women's full and equal power at peace tables, in parliaments, in boardrooms, in every room where decisions are made. Put women at the heart of peace and humanitarian action, because when crisis strikes, they lead the way. Make women and girls the driving force of climate action, especially rural and indigenous leaders who hold the key to a sustainable future. and across all these areas, ensure that we engage young women and girls. Excellencies, as we mark this anniversary, let it be a call to shape the future and ensure that the promises made in Beijing are not only remembered, but fully realized. Let us act with urgency. Let us act with courage. And let us deliver for all women and girls everywhere, leaving no one behind. I thank you.

Thank you, your excellencies, distinguished participants. Before I give the floor to our panellists, I would like to reiterate my warmest greetings to them and to emphasise the importance of their contributions feeding into our collective reflection. We need to have an interactive, enriching discussion with all participants, and it's therefore an honour for me to give the floor to Doreen Bogdan-Martin, Secretary General of the ITU. Madame, you have the floor. Thank you, President.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. As we look back to 1995, the year the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action was adopted, think about what the digital world looked like. Less than 2% of the world's population had a mobile phone. Less than 1%, or actually to be precise, 0.8%, about 40 million people at the time, were online, had access to the internet. Delegates to the Fourth World Conference on Women may not have referenced the internet or the mobile phone, but they did understand and recognize this well, the immense potential of technology and its ability to empower women and girls. The outcome document mentions technology 31 times. Ten years later, we held the World Summit on the Information Society in Tunis, and there member states acknowledged the full participation of women in the information society as necessary, necessary to ensure inclusiveness and respect for human rights. By 2005, 34% of the world's population had a mobile phone, and about 15%, 1 billion, were connected to the internet. But not Rebecca, an inspiring fashion designer from Ethiopia. She never made a mobile phone call. She didn't have access to the internet. But a few years ago, after receiving digital skills training from the ITU and the Enhanced Integrated Framework, Rebecca was able to launch Helmi, her e-commerce business that now reaches customers all over the world. And Rebecca's story is one of progress, progress in leveraging digital technologies to advance opportunities for women and girls everywhere. This progress was re-energized when Beijing plus 15 review took place and member states decided to encourage the implementation of women's economic empowerment policies that leverage digital technologies for lifelong education. 30 years after Beijing, parity in the Internet, parity in Internet use has been achieved in some places, in some regions, but the digital gender divide is far from closed. And I think, referring to the words of the President of the General Assembly, that is one of the hard truths. We have not closed the digital gender gap. And in least developed countries, the gap is actually getting bigger, with less than 30% of women having access to the internet. Closing this digital divide is a matter of empowerment. But, ladies and gentlemen, it also makes economic sense. While estimates vary, exact estimates vary, Connecting more women could boost global GDP by billions and billions of dollars. But connecting women to the internet is not enough. We have what we call a usage gap, compounded by other barriers that are facing women and girls from a digital skills deficit, affordability challenges, that smartphone is too expensive or the cost of service is too expensive. to unsafe online environments, to an underrepresentation in STEM education, just to name a few. The impact of these barriers is clear. If we look at computer science studies alone, the proportion of female graduates back when computer science came on the scene in the 80s was about 30 something percent. Today, it's about the same. we have not been able to attract more women and girls into STEM fields. Beyond education, women are underrepresented in the tech force, around 30%. And to note that just 2% of all startup funding goes to women-led tech ventures. Of course, in the AI sphere, the numbers are not much better, with women representing some 30% of the workforce when it comes to AI. And when it comes to women in leadership in government positions, when it comes to tech, it's about 20%. Ladies and gentlemen, I think you will all agree that women's unique perspective is absolutely vital if digital policy and tech innovation is to truly benefit all. When this happens, I think the results are inspiring. Look no further than Not a Woman's Job, which is a photo exhibition that was on display first here at UNOG and now is being hosted by the ITU, celebrating 100 incredible scientists, engineers, and technologists who just happen to be women. One of them is 22-year-old Mary from Uganda, who wants to become a great engineer to help other girls turn their dreams into reality. Another is Aniri. She's a single mother learning digital skills at a STEM center in South Sudan. Our ITU-led AI Skills Coalition is designed to help women like Mary and like Aniri access training opportunities at a time when 40% of global employment is exposed to artificial intelligence. Excellencies, as the UNSG mentioned this morning, let's continue leveraging the Global Digital Compact and the Pact of the Future, where member states reaffirm their commitment to the Beijing Declaration and the Platform for Action. ITU is

...firmly committed to continuing its role as a founding partner of the Equals Global Partnership, as an international gender champion, as a co-lead of the Generation Equality Action Coalition on Technology and Innovation, as a promoter of our Girls in ICT Day and World Telecommunications and Information Society Day on the 17th of May this year, when the ITU turns 160 years years old. Our anniversary theme, as agreed by our member states, is how digital transformation can empower women and girls like Rebecca, Mary, and Anieri. So much is possible when we work together. In fact, the only way to fully realize the promise of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action and to eliminate all divides, the digital divide, once and for all, is by working together in partnership on behalf of women and girls everywhere. Thank you.
Thank you. I now have the honor. of giving the floor to another Rebecca, Ms. Rebecca Greenspan, Secretary General of UNCTAD. Madam, you have the floor. Thank you, President.

So let me first honor the memory of all those women that were in Beijing. 30,000 women or more were in Beijing, and they were able to put together the most comprehensive policy agenda ever created for achieving gender equality. Whatever we have achieved was not made by the invisible hand. It was made by the voice, by the work, by the leadership of all those women that paved the way for us to be here today, and we have to honor them. My second point is how this really affected all of us. I was vice president of Costa Rica in 1995. So I know firsthand how Beijing affected us in our policies, in what we did. I can tell you that because of Beijing and Costa Rica already had in 1995, a law for the equality of men and women. But Beijing really pushed our agenda much further. First of all, it inspired us to put together the first plan to mainstream women perspective across all sectors of government. And that really took away the women work and program from a corner, because it was a corner of the government. And suddenly it became really a mainstream challenge for all the sectors of government. So after Beijing, we established and implemented our first across-the-board, across all sector of government, strategy to be implemented by everybody. And because of Beijing, we clearly widened the perspective of policies across the board to look at women equality in political, in social, in economy and cultural rights. And it was the first time, and Beijing was the first time, where it was really established that the economy and the global economy were not gender neutral. It was, you know, the economy and the global economy were gender blind, but not gender neutral. And we started to really look at the different impacts of policies on women and men, because policies have different impact. But we didn't study it before. We didn't have the data to establish the facts. And so this revolution, this data revolution, was initiated to really make women visible, to count women, to desegregate data. And so through it, we were able to establish research and programs in the universities, women programs, research programs, to really establish the facts, not precluding what we will find, but at least having the possibility to understand reality, what really was happening in the ground. And that was essential to be able to establish the differentiated impact of shocks on women and girls and on all of us, because also there are differentiated effects and impacts on men. Because Beijing clearly established the need to include women's studies. in research programs to understand better the discrimination mechanisms and the different realities on the ground. Because one of the things that also happened in Beijing is that we understood also that the word women doesn't say all about all the women, that there were different realities, that agendas had to be built from the bottom up. not from the top down. And this possibility of research, of data, of disaggregation, really made the challenges much more closer to the possibility of policy, to have the right policies to really confront the challenges that we were seeing on the ground. And by put on the center of the challenges that we face, gender violence, and it was said by everybody today, in all the different realms, in conflict, in society, in our homes. And so that was like the third revolution, yes, not only the data revolution and the fact that we established that the economy and the global economy was not neutral towards gender, but also the revolution in the laws. Because, you know, in many parts of the world, Till then, domestic violence was a private issue, not a public issue. And so we were able to make a legal revolution also. And they are asking me to speed. And so let me go to my final point. When we think about how it affected us, as I said, in my own country then, we were aware of the mechanisms for the training and follow up of the legal system, of the judicial system, to really comply with the gender violence laws against violence against women. And then the training and the institutional development also took off. So the gender mechanisms and the legal mechanisms and CEDAW as a very important part of the international institutionality to follow on Beijing. So let me just say to finish that the Beijing agenda was an agenda against discrimination. against discrimination against women. It was not an agenda for discrimination. It was an agenda against discrimination. So let me finish by reminding everyone that eliminating the discrimination against women is key, and we are not there yet. Today, 30 years later, in developed and developing countries, Even at the law level, we continue to have unacceptable discriminatory laws. 2.4 billion women don't have the same economic rights than men across 178 countries. So, Beijing gave us a foundation of rights. We must continue building here in the Human Rights Council. We must move from the declaration to implementation, from promises to practice, to building a world where women's rights, all rights, are truly universal, indivisible, and inalienable. Thank you.
Thank you very much. Thank you to the Secretary General, Vang Tai, and I now have the honor of giving the floor to Ms. Nala Haidar. Madam, you have the floor. Thank you, Your Excellency.

It is very difficult to take the floor after those wonderful speeches and referring also to CDAO, and I'm here humbly going to share with you also how CDAO celebrating this 30th anniversary. of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, which, as was stated by all the speakers, is indeed a landmark agreement that has been instrumental in advancing women's and girls' rights since 1995. The Beijing Platform for Action comprehensive approach addressing 12 critical areas of concern has indeed, as was illustrated, guided policies and programs worldwide. We have witnessed significant progress in areas that were alluded to, including institutional mechanism, gender parity in primary schools, et cetera. However, the challenges persist, and even worse, the backlash against the rights are worrying. Underrepresentation of women in decision-making and new forms of violence and misinformation. As we reflect on the past three decades, we must renew our commitments to gender equality, combat these challenges, and explore emerging issues like online violence to ensure that the Beijing Platform for Action remains relevant and effective tool for future generations. While we acknowledge the progress since the Beijing Platform for Action, we must also confront the evolving challenges. and these new forms of online and technology-facilitated violence, but at the same time, as was stated by the Secretary General of ITU, the opportunity that technology can afford women. We have to really turn our urgent attention to all these issues, as emerging technology, including AI algorithm, could set back or could lead to some discrimination, but there are also opportunities for positive change. The Beijing Platform for Action and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, CEDAW, have worked in tandem for the past 30 years. As you know, CEDAW predated the Beijing Platform for Action, but has really used the Beijing Platform for Action to provide a comprehensive framework. Because CEDAW, being a legally binding instrument, is the strongest mechanism for the protection, promotion, and fulfillment of women's And CEDAW can hold States Parties accountable, and some of you in the room have seen that recently in some of the dialogue, but also accompany the State Party to measure the progress and reinforce commitment. Through constructive dialogues and recommendations, CEDAW is the voice for millions of women. Its general recommendations, which are soft law tools, cover all the 12 critical areas of the Beijing Platform for Action. addressing women in poverty, education, healthcare, violence, armed conflict, political participation, and more. Crucially, CEDAW addresses emerging issues like the amplified stereotype in the area of technology so that the Beijing Platform for Action remains relevant. I was stated technology was cited, but we were not aware of where we are going to be 30 years after that. So I will not take you too much into the respective area, but I want to highlight because it's an opportunity for me talking to this August audience of state parties to say how much. It is important when we look at women and poverty, when we look at the link, the role of women in economic development, to look also at those general recommendations that have been provided by CDAO over the years. And we have now about, we have 40 C general recommendations that has been adopted. But I want to quote here on women and poverty, in particular general recommendation number 34. on rural women and general recommendation number 29 on economic consequences of marriage, which further solidify the connection that the Beijing Platform for Action has. alluded to. On education, again, I cannot quote enough the general recommendation number 36, where the whole issue of minimal number of girls in STEMs, where the whole issue of not being able to reverse this trend is still with us and is still a big challenge. Yet we have some guidance to state party who would like to address that in that soft law tool. Women and health, the same. Even if we are not very happy anymore with our general recommendation 24, because we have evolved much beyond that in jurisprudence on the bodily autonomy and because of the threat on sexual and reproductive health and rights, we are very concerned and we are already considering to update the general recommendation to take into account all these development. The same applies to violence, which is the fourth area of the Beijing Platform for Action. And there again, two general recommendation that are landmarks 19, but in particular 35, that has also alluded to feminicide and all the development around this issue. Women and armed conflict, same again here, this very important first general recommendation number 30 on this issue. When we remember that the preamble of CEDAW is about role of women in peace, and we seem to have departed from that for many, many years. So Bringing back the centrality of all of this, the same applies to women in leadership and decision-making, and many of you have been witness of the launch of GR40 last year on parity and the importance for all of us to continue addressing the challenge on women political representation. On institutional mechanism and for the advancement of women, I think the dialogue with state party show how important it is to accompany the state in what they are to move from legal framework to application, from de jure to de facto equality. And when it comes to the ninth area of the Beijing Platform for Action on human rights of women, we believe that CEDAW is at the core of this area of concern. CEDAW has sensitized and echoed crucial instruments and milestones, notably the Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action of 1993, which reaffirmed that the human rights of women and of the girl child are an inalienable, integral, and indivisible part of universal human rights, emphasizing that women's rights are human rights as a core belief and a driver for achieving progress.
